title: Islamic Baby Boy Names with Meanings: 60 Timeless and Modern Choices
seoTitle: Islamic Baby Boy Names with Meanings (60 Choices)
subtitle: Prophets, companions, divine-name compounds and classic Arabic virtue names — with what each name means and how to check it.
excerpt: 60 Islamic baby boy names with meanings: prophets' names, the Prophet's companions, Abd- names and Arabic virtue names, plus the hadith guidance on naming.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Choosing a name for a Muslim baby boy usually starts with one question: what does it mean? Islamic tradition puts meaning first. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have changed names whose meanings were poor, and Muslim families have always favoured names that honour God, the prophets and the early believers, or that describe a quality a parent hopes the child will grow into.

This guide brings together 60 well-established Islamic boy names in five groups — prophets' names, names of the Prophet's family and companions, names built on the divine names, classic Arabic virtue names, and short modern favourites — with the meaning most commonly given for each. Where scholars or dictionaries disagree about a meaning, we say so rather than pick the most flattering version. Every linked name opens its full NameVerse profile with the Arabic script and pronunciation where our record holds them.
keyTakeaways: Islamic naming guidance centres on good meaning: names that honour God or the prophets, or describe a virtue.
In a hadith recorded by Muslim, the Prophet said the names most beloved to God are Abdullah and Abdur-Rahman.
Names of the prophets — Ibrahim, Yusuf, Musa, Isa, Yahya — are used across the Muslim world and are shared with Jewish and Christian tradition.
Some divine names (Allah, ar-Rahman) are reserved for God and are only used in Abd- compounds; ask a scholar if you are unsure about a name.
Arabic names have several English spellings; choose one and use it consistently on every document.

sections.title: What Islamic tradition says about naming a boy
sections.content:
The clearest guidance comes from the hadith collections. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet is reported as saying that the most beloved names to God are Abdullah (servant of God) and Abdur-Rahman (servant of the Most Merciful). Other reports describe him changing names with harsh or unsuitable meanings and warning against names that claim greatness belonging to God alone — the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari singles out "king of kings" (Malik al-Amlak) as the worst of names.

On timing, two practices are both reported from the Sunnah: naming on the day of birth — the Prophet named his own son Ibrahim on the night he was born — and naming on the seventh day, together with the aqiqah sacrifice and the shaving of the baby's hair. Families follow either, and many announce the name at the aqiqah.

Beyond that, the field is wide. A Muslim boy's name does not have to be Arabic or appear in the Quran; scholars generally accept any name with a good meaning that does not imply worship of anything other than God. That is why Persian, Turkish, Urdu and other names sit comfortably alongside Arabic ones in Muslim families around the world.

sections.title: Names of the prophets
sections.content: Prophets' names are the backbone of Muslim boys' naming. The Quran names 25 prophets, most of whom also appear in the Hebrew Bible or the New Testament, so their names carry Hebrew or Aramaic roots with Arabic forms. Muhammad itself is the most widely used of all: in England and Wales, for example, it was the most popular boys' name registered in 2023, according to the Office for National Statistics. Our separate guide to the 25 prophets covers every name in detail; these are the ones most often given today.

sections.title: Names of the Prophet's family and companions
sections.content: The second great source of Muslim boys' names is the first generation of believers — the Prophet's family and his companions (the Sahaba). These names are Arabic in origin, many predate Islam, and most carry plain, concrete meanings. A family that chooses Ali or Umar is usually honouring the person rather than the dictionary sense, but the meanings are worth knowing.

names.name: Ali
names.note: The Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, the fourth caliph

names.name: Husayn
names.meaning: "Little good one", a diminutive of Hasan

names.name: Zayd
names.note: The only companion named in the Quran (33:37)

names.name: Salman
names.note: Salman al-Farsi was a Persian companion

names.name: Ammar
names.meaning: One who builds up or brings life to a place

sections.title: Abd- names built on the names of God
sections.content:
A large family of Muslim names joins "Abd" (servant) to one of the divine names traditionally counted among the 99 Names of God: Abdullah, Abdur-Rahman, Abdul-Karim and so on. Because they describe the child as a servant of God, they are among the most recommended names of all.

Two points of etiquette come up often. First, some divine names — Allah and ar-Rahman above all — are reserved for God, so they are used only in Abd- compounds and never as a standalone name. Second, many other divine names are also ordinary Arabic adjectives: karim (generous), hadi (guide), aziz (mighty, dear), malik (king). These are widely used as given names on their own, and most scholars accept that, though some families prefer the Abd- form as a sign of respect. If you are unsure, ask a scholar you trust.

In everyday speech these names are often shortened, and the article in the middle changes with the next letter — Abdur-Rahman, Abdus-Salam, Abdul-Aziz — which is why you will see many spellings of the same name.

names.name: Abdus-Salam
names.meaning: Servant of the Source of Peace

sections.title: Classic Arabic virtue and character names
sections.content: Many of the most loved Muslim names simply name a quality: generosity, guidance, nobility, light. They work across Arabic-, Urdu-, Persian- and Turkish-speaking families and are easy to explain to a child later. A few have a Quranic connection — Tariq is the name of Surah 86 — while others, such as Rayyan, come from the hadith: al-Rayyan is the gate of Paradise through which those who fasted will enter, according to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.

names.name: Rayyan
names.meaning: Well-watered, luxuriant; name of a gate of Paradise in hadith
names.note: From the hadith, not the Quran

names.name: Imran
names.meaning: Prosperity; name of the family of Maryam (Surah 3, Al Imran)

names.name: Hadi
names.meaning: Guide, one who leads to the right path

sections.title: Spelling and pronunciation: choosing an English form
sections.content:
Arabic script and the Latin alphabet do not match letter for letter, so every Arabic name has several defensible English spellings: Yusuf, Yousuf, Youssef; Hamza, Hamzah; Zayd, Zaid. None is wrong. What matters is consistency — use the same spelling on the birth certificate, passport, school records and any religious documents, because a mismatch can cause real administrative trouble later.

If your child will grow up in an English-speaking country, it also helps to know which sounds English lacks. Letters such as 'ayn, the throaty h of Hasan and the q of Tariq are approximated by most English speakers. Names built mostly from shared sounds — Adam, Zayn, Idris, Yusuf, Bilal — are the ones most likely to be pronounced close to the Arabic by teachers and friends. Many families choose such a name, or pair a less familiar first name with an easier middle name.
bullets: Pick one spelling and use it on every official document.
Say the full name aloud with your surname and listen for awkward rhymes or initials.
Check the meaning in Arabic, not just a one-word English gloss.
Ask a scholar or imam about any name whose connotations you are unsure of.

sections.title: Names to avoid or check first
sections.content:
A handful of names are best avoided on religious grounds. Names that ascribe divine attributes to a person, such as Malik al-Amlak (king of kings), are explicitly discouraged in the hadith. Names of figures the Quran condemns — Fir'awn (Pharaoh), Haman, Qarun — are not used for obvious reasons. Names that declare servitude to anyone other than God (for example Abd an-Nabi, servant of the Prophet) are discouraged by many scholars, even though they have historically been used in some regions.

Finally, check the meaning of any name you find on a list in at least two places. Popular name lists sometimes repeat attractive but unsupported meanings. Our profiles show the meaning recorded in our database; if you find a better source, we would like to hear about it.

faqs.q: What is the most recommended Islamic name for a boy?
faqs.a: In a hadith recorded in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad said the names most beloved to God are Abdullah and Abdur-Rahman. More broadly, names of the prophets and names with a clearly good meaning are recommended.

faqs.q: Does a Muslim boy's name have to be Arabic?
faqs.a: No. Scholars generally accept any name with a good meaning that does not imply worship of anything other than God. Muslim families widely use Persian, Turkish, Urdu, Malay and other names alongside Arabic ones.

faqs.q: When should a Muslim baby be named?
faqs.a: Both practices are reported from the Sunnah: naming on the day of birth, as the Prophet did with his son Ibrahim, and naming on the seventh day together with the aqiqah. Families follow either.

faqs.q: Can I name my son Muhammad?
faqs.a: Yes. Muhammad is one of the most widely used boys' names in the Muslim world. In some countries, particularly in South Asia, it is often combined with a second name that the boy is called by day to day, such as Muhammad Ali or Muhammad Yusuf.

faqs.q: Is it allowed to use a divine name like Karim or Hadi on its own?
faqs.a: Many divine names are also ordinary Arabic adjectives (karim means generous, hadi means guide) and are widely used as given names on their own. Names reserved for God, such as Allah and ar-Rahman, are used only in Abd- compounds. Ask a scholar if you are unsure about a specific name.

content.introduction:
Muslim parents choosing a girl's name tend to look in three places: the women honoured in Islamic history, Arabic words for the qualities they hope their daughter will have, and the natural world — flowers, light, the moon. All three are well represented in this guide.

Below are 60 Islamic girl names with the meaning most commonly given for each. We note when a meaning is disputed (several of the most famous names have older, more literal senses than the poetic glosses found on name lists) and when a name has a Quranic connection. Linked names open their full NameVerse profile, with Arabic script and pronunciation where our record holds them.
keyTakeaways: Maryam is the only woman mentioned by name in the Quran; Fatima, Aisha and Khadija honour early Muslim women but do not appear in the Quran.
The hadith record the Prophet changing girls' names with unsuitable meanings — Barrah ("pious", which sounded like self-praise) became Zaynab.
Arabic virtue names such as Iman (faith), Huda (guidance) and Amal (hope) are short, meaningful and easy to pronounce in many languages.
Several famous names have literal meanings that differ from popular glosses; families choose them for the woman they honour, not the dictionary sense.

sections.title: How Muslim families choose a girl's name
sections.content:
The guidance that applies to boys applies equally to girls: choose a name with a good meaning, avoid names that imply arrogance or claim divine qualities, and avoid names tied to idols. The hadith collections preserve two well-known examples. A girl named 'Asiyah (a word that can mean "disobedient") was renamed Jamilah, "beautiful". And Zaynab bint Abi Salamah was originally called Barrah, "pious" — the Prophet changed it because the name praised its bearer, saying that God knows best who is truly righteous.

The practical lesson for parents is to read a name's meaning in Arabic, not only its English translation, and to prefer names whose meaning is a hope or a quality rather than a boast. Names of righteous women, virtues and beautiful things in nature all pass that test easily.

sections.title: Women honoured in Islamic history
sections.content: These names belong to the Prophet's family, his wives and companions, and to women the Quran and hadith praise. A few have literal meanings that surprise people — Khadijah means a child born early, Fatimah one who weans — but families choose them to honour the women who bore them, and they remain among the most loved Muslim names in the world.

sections.title: Arabic virtue names
sections.content: Virtue names are the quiet favourites of Muslim girls' naming: short, positive and full of meaning. Many of these words occur in the Quran — sakinah is the tranquillity God sends down on believers, huda is guidance, rahmah is mercy — which gives the names a scriptural echo without being names of people.

sections.title: Names from light, flowers and the night sky
sections.content: Arabic and Persian give Muslim families a rich vocabulary of nature names. Some are Arabic (Noor, Zahra, Layla); others are Persian words long used across the Muslim world (Yasmin, Gul, Nargis, Sitara). Lina is a lovely, little-known Quranic example: līnah is the word for a palm tree in Surah al-Hashr (59:5).

names.name: Qamar

sections.title: Spelling, pronunciation and names that travel
sections.content:
If your daughter will grow up speaking English as well as Arabic, Urdu or another language, it is worth thinking about how her name will be said at school. Names built from sounds both languages share — Sara, Layla, Noor, Hana, Lina, Maryam — are usually pronounced close to the original. Names with 'ayn or the deep h (Aisha, Huda, Rahma) are perfectly usable but will be approximated by English speakers.

Spelling is a separate choice. Fatimah or Fatima, Safiyya or Safiya, Aisha or Ayesha: each is correct, and the choice often reflects a family's language background. Pick one and keep it identical on every official document.
bullets: Read the name's meaning in Arabic, not just a one-word English gloss.
Prefer meanings that express a hope or quality rather than a boast.
Check how the name sounds with your family name and any middle name.
Use one spelling consistently on the birth certificate, passport and school records.

sections.title: Names to think twice about
sections.content:
A few categories of names are discouraged on religious grounds: names that praise their bearer's piety in a boastful way (the reason Barrah became Zaynab), names of pre-Islamic idols such as al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, and names of women the Quran presents negatively. Separately, some words that appear in the Quran are unsuitable as names because of their context, so a Quranic word is not automatically a good name. Our guide to Quranic names covers this in more detail.

If you find a beautiful name with an unusual meaning on a list, look it up in a second source before you decide. Name lists sometimes repeat attractive but unsupported meanings; our profiles show the meaning recorded in our database and welcome corrections.

faqs.q: Which women are named in the Quran?
faqs.a: Only one woman is mentioned by name in the Quran: Maryam, the mother of Isa (Jesus). Surah 19 is named after her. Other women, such as the wife of Pharaoh and the mother of Musa, are referred to without being named.

faqs.q: Are Fatima, Aisha and Khadija Quranic names?
faqs.a: No. They are names of women in the Prophet's family — his daughter Fatimah and his wives Aisha and Khadijah — and are among the most loved Muslim names, but the names themselves do not appear in the Quran.

faqs.q: What does Zaynab mean?
faqs.a: Its meaning is debated. Some dictionaries connect it to a fragrant plant; a popular explanation reads it as zayn ab, "the adornment of her father". Both are given in naming references.

faqs.q: Is Layla an Islamic name?
faqs.a: Layla is an Arabic name meaning "night", known from classical Arabic poetry such as the story of Layla and Majnun. It is widely used by Muslim families and has a good meaning, so it is generally considered a suitable Islamic name.

faqs.q: Can a Muslim girl have a non-Arabic name?
faqs.a: Yes. Any name with a good meaning is generally accepted. Persian names such as Yasmin, Nargis and Sitara, and Turkish names such as Elif and Ayla, are widely used by Muslim families.

title: The 25 Prophets Named in the Quran: Prophet Names for Baby Boys

subtitle: Every prophet named in the Quran, with the Arabic name, its English equivalent, its meaning and how the name is used today.

author: NameVerse Editorial Team

content.introduction:
Naming a son after a prophet is one of the oldest Muslim naming customs, and it has the clearest possible precedent: the Prophet Muhammad named his own son Ibrahim, saying he had named him after his forefather. The Quran mentions 25 prophets by name. Muslims believe there were many more — the Quran itself says every community was sent a messenger — but these 25 are the names a Muslim family can take directly from scripture.

Most of them are shared with Judaism and Christianity, which is why Yusuf and Joseph, or Dawud and David, are the same name in different languages. Below you will find all 25, with the Arabic form, the English equivalent, the meaning usually given and notes on how each name is used today.
keyTakeaways: The Quran names 25 prophets; Muslims believe many more were sent.
The Prophet Muhammad named his own son Ibrahim, a clear precedent for prophets' names.
Most prophet names have Hebrew or Aramaic roots and are shared with Jewish and Christian tradition.
A few — Hud, Shu'ayb, Dhul-Kifl, Lut — are rarely used as given names today.

sections.title: All 25 prophets named in the Quran
sections.content: The list below follows the order in which the prophets are usually presented, from Adam to Muhammad. Meanings for names with Hebrew roots are the standard etymologies given in biblical reference works; where a name's original meaning is uncertain or debated, we say so. English equivalents are given where a figure is widely identified with a biblical prophet, but for Dhul-Kifl and Shu'ayb those identifications are traditional opinions rather than certainties.

sections.title: The prophet names families choose most
sections.content:
Some prophet names are everyday names across the Muslim world; others are honoured but rarely given. Muhammad stands apart: it is used so widely that in many South Asian families it is paired with a second name the boy is called day to day — Muhammad Ali, Muhammad Yusuf — and in England and Wales it was the most popular boys' name registered in 2023, according to the Office for National Statistics.

After Muhammad, the prophet names most often given are Ibrahim, Yusuf, Musa, Isa, Adam, Ismail, Yahya, Zakariya, Idris, Ilyas, Yunus, Dawud and Sulayman. They share three useful qualities: they are short, their meanings are well documented, and they are recognisable to Christian and Jewish neighbours through their biblical forms.

Salih and Harun are used less often but are entirely conventional. Hud, Shu'ayb and Lut are honoured as prophets but are rarely chosen as names, and Dhul-Kifl is a title rather than a given name.

sections.title: Prophet names across Islam, Judaism and Christianity
sections.content:
Because most of these prophets also appear in the Bible, the same name often exists in three forms. That can be a gift for families who live in mixed communities or want a name that is easy to explain: a boy named Yusuf can tell friends his name is Joseph in English, and Dawud can point to David.

The pairs are: Adam and Adam; Nuh and Noah; Ibrahim and Abraham; Lut and Lot; Ismail and Ishmael; Ishaq and Isaac; Yaqub and Jacob; Yusuf and Joseph; Ayyub and Job; Musa and Moses; Harun and Aaron; Dawud and David; Sulayman and Solomon; Ilyas and Elijah; Al-Yasa and Elisha; Yunus and Jonah; Zakariya and Zechariah; Yahya and John; Isa and Jesus. Idris is widely identified with Enoch, though that identification is a matter of interpretation.

Some families deliberately choose the Arabic form to mark the name as Islamic; others use the shared form, such as Adam or Ilyas/Elias, precisely because it works in every community they belong to.

sections.title: Spellings you will see
sections.content:
Arabic names reach English through transliteration, so expect variation. Common forms include Ibrahim and Ebrahim; Yusuf, Yousuf and Youssef; Ismail and Ismael; Ishaq and Ishak; Yaqub and Yakub; Dawud, Dawood and Daud; Sulayman, Suleiman and Sulaiman; Zakariya, Zakariyya and Zakaria; Isa and Eisa. Regional pronunciation shapes these choices too — Turkish families write Yusuf, İbrahim and Süleyman, while South Asian families often prefer Yousuf and Sulaiman.

There is no single correct spelling. Choose the form that matches how your family says the name, and keep it identical on every document.
bullets: Muhammad: Mohammed, Muhammed, Mohamed, Mohammad
Yusuf: Yousuf, Youssef, Yousef
Sulayman: Suleiman, Sulaiman, Süleyman
Zakariya: Zakariyya, Zakaria, Zachariah (English)

sections.title: Etiquette and practical questions
sections.content:
There is no religious objection to naming a boy after a prophet; the practice is recommended. Two customs are worth knowing. First, many families treat the name Muhammad with particular respect — avoiding nicknames that shorten or alter it — and some add a second name for everyday use. Second, when a prophet's name is mentioned in speech or writing, Muslims customarily add the blessing 'alayhi as-salam (peace be upon him), and for the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam. That custom applies to the prophet, not to a child who shares his name.

If you want a prophet's name that is less common in your community, consider Ilyas, Yahya, Zakariya, Idris or Harun — all fully established names with clear meanings.

faqs.q: How many prophets are named in the Quran?
faqs.a: Twenty-five prophets are mentioned by name in the Quran. Muslims believe many more prophets were sent; the Quran states that every community received a messenger.

faqs.q: Is it allowed to name a baby after a prophet?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is recommended. The Prophet Muhammad named his own son Ibrahim after the prophet Abraham, as recorded in Sahih Muslim.

faqs.q: What is the Arabic name for Jesus?
faqs.a: In the Quran, Jesus is called Isa (often written Eisa in English). It is a common Muslim boy's name.

faqs.q: Which prophet names are rarely used for babies?
faqs.a: Hud, Shu'ayb and Lut are honoured as prophets but are rarely given as names, and Dhul-Kifl is a title rather than a given name. The others are all in regular use.

faqs.q: Who is the prophet Idris?
faqs.a: Idris is a prophet mentioned twice in the Quran (19:56 and 21:85). Many Muslim scholars identify him with the biblical Enoch, though that identification is a matter of interpretation. Idris is a popular boys' name.

content.introduction:
Many lists sold as "Quranic names" are really lists of Islamic names in general. That matters if you specifically want a name taken from the Quran: Fatima, Aisha, Khadija, Zainab and Hafsa are beloved Muslim names, but none of them occurs in the Quran. Maryam is the only woman the Quran names.

This guide sorts genuinely Quranic names into three groups — people named in the Quran, Arabic words from the Quran that families use as names, and the titles of surahs — and adds a short section on Quranic words that are best avoided as names because of their context. sections.title: Islamic versus Quranic: why the difference matters
sections.content:
An Islamic name is any name Muslims use that has a suitable meaning. A Quranic name is narrower: the name, or the word it is built from, actually occurs in the text of the Quran. Most families do not need that narrower category — Islamic guidance asks for good meaning, not Quranic origin — but some parents want it, and it helps to know which names qualify.

The most common surprise is that the names of the Prophet's family are mostly not Quranic. His daughters (Fatimah, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum) and wives (Khadijah, Aishah, Hafsah) are not named in the text. Even Rayyan, often listed as Quranic, comes from the hadith: al-Rayyan is the gate of Paradise reserved for those who fasted, according to Sahih al-Bukhari. These are excellent names; they simply belong to the wider Islamic tradition.

sections.title: Quranic words and surah titles used as boys' names
sections.content: Boys' names drawn from the Quran include prophets' names, a few words for qualities and light, and the titles of surahs. Taha and Yasin deserve a special note. They are among the disconnected letters (al-muqatta'at) that open certain surahs, and their meaning is not explained in the text. Popular tradition treats them as names of the Prophet; many scholars point out there is no authentic evidence for that, while still accepting their use as given names, which is widespread in South Asia and the Arab world.

sections.title: Quranic words that are not good names
sections.content:
Because the Quran describes Hell and its punishments, condemned peoples and tyrants as well as Paradise and virtue, some of its words are clearly unsuitable as names. Fir'awn (Pharaoh), Haman, Qarun and Abu Lahab are obvious examples. Less obvious are words that sound pleasant to non-Arabic speakers but carry harsh meanings in context — ghassaq, for instance, is a foul drink of the people of Hell (78:25), yet it has occasionally been chosen as a name from lists that gave no context.

The safe approach is simple: before choosing a Quranic word as a name, read the verse in a translation and, if possible, ask someone who reads Arabic. A name list that gives a single English word without a verse reference is not enough to go on.

sections.title: How to check a Quranic name yourself
sections.content:
You do not need to be a scholar to verify that a name is Quranic. Search for the word on Quran.com, which lets you search the Arabic text and read several English translations of each verse. Look at where the word appears and in what context, and note the exact Arabic spelling — many names have near-identical relatives with different meanings.

For names of people, our profiles note when a name is linked to a Quranic figure. If you find an error in a meaning or a reference, please tell us so we can correct it at the source record.
bullets: Search the Arabic word on Quran.com and read at least two translations.
Check the context: is the word praised, neutral or condemned?
Note the exact Arabic spelling and the vowels.
Remember that a name does not have to be Quranic to be a good Islamic name.

faqs.q: Which girls' names are in the Quran?
faqs.a: Only one woman, Maryam, is named in the Quran. Many girls' names are Quranic words rather than names of people — Noor, Huda, Iman, Rahma, Sakina, Bushra, Jannah, Kawthar, Tasnim and Salsabil are examples.

faqs.q: Is Rayyan a Quranic name?
faqs.a: No. Rayyan comes from the hadith: al-Rayyan is described in Sahih al-Bukhari as the gate of Paradise for those who fasted. It is a good Islamic name, but the word does not occur in the Quran.

faqs.q: Are Taha and Yasin names of the Prophet?
faqs.a: Popular tradition says so, but many scholars note there is no authentic evidence. Both are disconnected letters (muqatta'at) that open Surahs 20 and 36. They are nonetheless widely accepted as given names.

faqs.q: Is it better to choose a Quranic name than an Islamic one?
faqs.a: Islamic guidance asks for a name with a good meaning; it does not require the name to come from the Quran. A Quranic name is a lovely choice, but names such as Fatima, Aisha and Khadija are equally valued.

faqs.q: How can I confirm a name appears in the Quran?
faqs.a: Search the Arabic word on Quran.com, read the verse in translation, and check the context. A trustworthy name source should give a verse reference.

title: Modern Muslim Baby Names: Short, Meaningful Names That Work Worldwide
seoTitle: Modern Muslim Baby Names for Boys and Girls
subtitle: Short, authentic Muslim names that are easy to say in Arabic, English, Urdu and Turkish — with their meanings and the checks worth doing.
excerpt: Modern Muslim baby names for boys and girls that are short, authentic and easy to pronounce worldwide — Zayn, Idris, Yusuf, Inaya, Aya, Noor and more.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide
seoKeywords: muslim names that are easy to pronounce

content.introduction:
"Modern" Muslim names are rarely new. What parents usually mean is a name that feels current: short, easy to spell, pronounced the same way by grandparents in Lahore or Cairo and by teachers in London or Toronto, and still rooted in a clear, good meaning. Many of the names that fit that brief are centuries old — Adam, Idris, Yusuf, Noor, Hana — which is exactly why they work.

This guide collects modern-feeling Muslim names for boys and girls, explains the meaning of each, and flags the handful of popular names whose meanings are uncertain. It also covers Turkish-style names such as Elif, Ayla and Emir, which have become favourites well beyond Turkey.
keyTakeaways: Most "modern" Muslim names are classic names with short, cross-language sounds.
Names built from sounds Arabic and English share — Adam, Zayn, Lina, Hana — are pronounced most consistently.
Turkish forms such as Elif, Ayla, Emir and Kerem are now widely used by Muslim families of many backgrounds.
Check the meaning of any trendy name in two sources: some popular glosses are unsupported.

sections.title: What makes a Muslim name feel modern
sections.content:
Looking at the names Muslim families choose today, a few patterns stand out. Short names of one or two syllables dominate. Names that exist in more than one tradition — Adam, Sara, Ilyas/Elias, Isa — are popular with families who live across cultures. And there is a clear preference for names whose meaning can be explained in a sentence: "Zayn means beauty", "Inaya means care".

There is also a practical side. Names with letters English lacks are perfectly good names, but they will be approximated outside Arabic-speaking communities. If you want a name that survives that intact, look for one made of sounds both languages share. None of this is a religious requirement — it is simply what many families weigh.

sections.title: Modern Muslim boy names
sections.content: Each of these names is established in Islamic tradition, short, and easy to pronounce in most languages. Several are prophets' names; others are classic Arabic words for good qualities.

names.meaning: The first prophet; "man", linked to earth

names.name: Rayan
names.meaning: Well-watered; linked to the gate of Paradise al-Rayyan

sections.title: Modern Muslim girl names
sections.content: Short virtue and nature names lead modern Muslim girls' naming. Many are Quranic words; others are classic Arabic names that have travelled well.

names.meaning: Sign, wonder; a verse of the Quran

names.name: Maryam
names.meaning: Mary; the only woman named in the Quran

sections.title: Turkish-style names popular across the Muslim world
sections.content: Turkish television and the large Turkish diaspora have made a set of Turkish names popular with Muslim families far beyond Turkey. Some are Turkish spellings of Arabic names (Emir from Amir, Kerem from Arabic karam, generosity); others are native Turkish words (Ayla, Deniz). Elif is the Turkish name of the first letter of the Arabic alphabet, alif.

names.meaning: Halo of light around the moon

sections.title: Popular names with uncertain meanings
sections.content:
A few very popular Muslim names circulate with meanings that are hard to confirm. Ayaan is often listed as "gift of God", but that sense is not well attested; Zara is variously explained as a form of Sarah ("princess") or as related to Arabic zahra (blossom, radiance). These names are widely used and perfectly acceptable — the point is simply not to choose them for a meaning you cannot confirm.

The same caution applies to any "unique Muslim name" found on a long list. If a list offers a beautiful meaning without a source, look the name up in an Arabic dictionary or ask someone who reads Arabic before you decide.

sections.title: What the data does and does not show
sections.content:
Popularity figures for Muslim names are patchy, because most national statistics do not record religion. Some signals exist: Muhammad was the most popular boys' name in England and Wales in 2023, according to the Office for National Statistics, and BabyCenter's in-progress 2026 table for the US includes Muhammad among its top 40 boys' names and Layla among its top 40 girls' names. Neither measures use within Muslim communities specifically — Layla, in particular, is chosen by families of many backgrounds.

For most parents, the more useful question is how a name will work for their own child: how it sounds with the family name, whether relatives can pronounce it, and whether its meaning is one the child will be glad to explain.

faqs.q: What are good modern Muslim boy names?
faqs.a: Short, established names with clear meanings work best: Adam, Zayn, Idris, Yusuf, Ilyas, Isa, Musa, Sami, Hadi, Malik, Ayman and Tamim are good examples.

faqs.q: What are good modern Muslim girl names?
faqs.a: Popular modern choices include Aya, Inaya, Noor, Hana, Lina, Layla, Iman, Alya, Amira, Maryam, Jana and Reem — all short, with good meanings.

faqs.q: Are Turkish names Islamic?
faqs.a: Turkish names such as Elif, Emir and Kerem are widely used by Muslim families. Some are Turkish forms of Arabic names; others are Turkish words with good meanings, which is what Islamic naming guidance asks for.

faqs.q: What does Ayaan mean?
faqs.a: Ayaan is commonly listed as meaning "gift of God", but that meaning is not well attested in standard references. It is widely used, especially in South Asia, but if the meaning matters to you, treat it as uncertain.

faqs.q: Is Zayn or Zain the correct spelling?
faqs.a: Both are correct transliterations of the same Arabic name, meaning beauty or grace. Choose the one that matches how your family writes it and use it consistently.

title: Persian Baby Names with Meanings: Poetic Names for Boys and Girls
seoTitle: Persian Baby Names with Meanings for Boys and Girls
subtitle: Names from Farsi, the Shahnameh and Persian poetry — used in Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and across Central Asia.
excerpt: Persian baby names with meanings: poetic girls' names like Laleh, Shirin and Parisa, heroic boys' names from the Shahnameh, and the word-parts behind them.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Persian has given the world some of its most musical names. Laleh (tulip), Shirin (sweet), Nasrin (wild rose), Darya (sea), Arman (aspiration) — many are ordinary Farsi words, chosen for their sound and imagery. Others come from Persian literature, above all Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, the national epic completed around the year 1010, whose heroes and heroines still name children in Iran and beyond.

Persian names are used far outside Iran. They are common in Afghanistan and Tajikistan, in Pakistan and India through centuries of Persian as a court and literary language, and among diaspora families worldwide. This guide explains the meanings of popular Persian names, the word-parts that build many of them, and a note on names with pre-Islamic, Zoroastrian roots.
keyTakeaways: Many Persian names are everyday Farsi words for flowers, light, the moon and good qualities.
Heroic names such as Rostam, Sohrab and Siavash come from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.
Word-parts recur: gol/gul (flower), mah (moon), naz (grace), shah (king), -zad (born of), mehr (love, sun).
Some Persian names (Dariush, Kourosh, Anahita) have pre-Islamic roots; Muslim families use them as cultural names.

sections.title: Where Persian names come from
sections.content:
Persian names fall into three broad groups. The largest is made of plain Farsi words — flowers, stars, seasons, qualities — such as Bahar (spring) or Omid (hope). The second comes from literature: the Shahnameh supplied Rostam, Sohrab, Tahmineh and Rudabeh, and later romances supplied names such as Shirin. The third is a set of ancient royal and religious names — Kourosh (Cyrus), Dariush (Darius), Anahita — that predate Islam and are used today as markers of Iranian heritage.

Persian has also absorbed a great many Arabic names, and Arabic has borrowed Persian ones (Yasmin, for example, is Persian). That is why the same name can appear on both Persian and Arabic lists. Where a name on this page is Arabic in origin, we say so.

sections.title: Persian girl names
sections.content: Persian girls' names are especially rich in flowers and light. Many combine two words — Mahnaz, "the grace of the moon"; Golnar, "pomegranate blossom" — which gives them their poetic quality.

names.meaning: Grace or glory of the moon

sections.title: Persian boy names
sections.content: Persian boys' names tend toward aspiration and victory — hope, success, triumph — alongside the great heroes of the Shahnameh. Several (Firuz, Shahzad, Bahadur) also became common in Urdu and in Indian Muslim families.

sections.title: Names from the Shahnameh
sections.content:
Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (Book of Kings) retells the history and legends of Iran from creation to the Arab conquest. Its characters have been naming children for a thousand years. The best-known are the hero Rostam and his tragic son Sohrab; Rostam's wife Tahmineh and his mother Rudabeh; the prince Siavash, a byword for innocence; and Kaveh the blacksmith, who led the revolt against the tyrant Zahhak. Gordafarid, a woman warrior who fights Sohrab, is a newer favourite for girls.

These names carry stories as much as meanings. Sohrab and Siavash both die young in the epic, which some families consider and others regard as irrelevant — the names are thoroughly established either way.

sections.title: The word-parts behind Persian names
sections.content: Once you know a few Persian elements, many names explain themselves — and you can judge whether a new combination you find online is real.
bullets: Gol / Gul — flower or rose: Golnar, Gulnaz, Gulshan (rose garden), Golbahar.
Mah — moon: Mahsa, Mahnaz, Mahtab (moonlight), Mahrukh (moon-faced).
Naz — grace, charm, pride: Mahnaz, Shahnaz, Gulnaz.
Shah — king: Shahzad (prince), Shahram, Shahin, Shahnaz.
-zad — born of: Behzad (well-born), Farzad, Shahzad.
-dad — given by: Mehrdad, Khodadad (given by God).
Mehr — love, kindness; also the sun and the old deity Mithra: Mehr, Mehrdad, Mehrnaz.
Roshan — bright: Roshan, Roshanak, Roshni (Urdu/Hindi).

sections.title: Persian names in Muslim families
sections.content:
Most Persian names are simply Persian words and carry no religious meaning, which is why Muslim families from Iran to India have used them for centuries alongside Arabic names. A small group — Anahita (an ancient Iranian water divinity), Mitra, Mehrdad and other names connected with Mithra, and royal names such as Kourosh and Dariush — have pre-Islamic, Zoroastrian-era associations. In Iran they are used today mainly as cultural, national names. Some religious families prefer to avoid names linked to pre-Islamic deities, so if that matters to you, look up a name's background before choosing it.

For pronunciation, remember that Persian vowels differ from English ones: the a in Laleh and Darya is broad, and kh (as in Khurshid) is the throaty sound of Scottish "loch".

faqs.q: Are Persian names Islamic?
faqs.a: Most Persian names are ordinary Persian words with good meanings, so they suit Islamic naming guidance and are widely used by Muslim families. A few have pre-Islamic religious associations; some families avoid those.

faqs.q: What are popular Persian girl names?
faqs.a: Well-loved Persian girls' names include Laleh (tulip), Nasrin (wild rose), Shirin (sweet), Parisa (like a fairy), Setareh (star), Darya (sea), Mahsa (like the moon) and Bahar (spring).

faqs.q: What are strong Persian boy names?
faqs.a: Arman (aspiration), Firuz (victorious), Bahadur (brave), Kamran (successful) and Shahin (falcon) are popular, as are Shahnameh heroes such as Rostam, Sohrab and Arash.

faqs.q: Is Yasmin Persian or Arabic?
faqs.a: Yasmin comes from the Persian word for jasmine (yasaman) and entered Arabic and many other languages from Persian.

faqs.q: What does Mahnoor mean?
faqs.a: Mahnoor combines Persian mah (moon) with Arabic noor (light), giving "moonlight" or "light of the moon". It is especially popular in Pakistan.

title: Hindu Baby Boy Names with Meanings: Traditional and Modern Sanskrit Names
seoTitle: Hindu Baby Boy Names with Meanings (Sanskrit)
subtitle: Names of gods and heroes, Vedic and Sanskrit virtue names, and modern favourites — with meanings, and notes where popular meanings are doubtful.
excerpt: Hindu baby boy names with meanings: names of deities and epic heroes, Sanskrit virtue names and modern favourites like Aarav and Vihaan — with honest notes.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Hindu boys' names draw on one of the deepest naming traditions in the world: Sanskrit, the Vedas and Upanishads, the great epics Ramayana and Mahabharata, and the many names and epithets of the gods. A single deity can supply dozens of names — Vishnu alone has a thousand in the Vishnu Sahasranama — and every Indian language adds its own forms and favourites.

This guide groups Hindu boy names into names of deities, heroes of the epics, Sanskrit virtue and nature names, and modern names that have become popular in the last two decades. For each we give the meaning usually recorded. Where a fashionable meaning does not match the classical Sanskrit sense, we say so, because a name's meaning is something your son may want to explain for the rest of his life.
keyTakeaways: The Hindu naming ceremony, Namakarana, is traditionally held on the tenth or twelfth day after birth.
Many families choose a name beginning with a syllable linked to the baby's birth nakshatra (lunar mansion).
Deity names and epithets — Krishna, Madhav, Shiv, Rudra, Ganesh, Kartik — are among the most enduring choices.
Some modern favourites carry popular meanings that differ from classical Sanskrit; check before you choose.

sections.title: How Hindu families choose a boy's name
sections.content:
The naming ceremony, Namakarana, is one of the sixteen samskaras (rites of passage). The Grihya Sutras place it on the tenth or twelfth day after birth, though families today hold it anywhere from the eleventh day to the first birthday. The classical texts give surprisingly detailed advice: a boy's name of two or four syllables was preferred, and names connected with a deity, a virtue, the family, a lucky star or a beautiful thing in nature were recommended, while inauspicious words were to be avoided.

Many families also consult the baby's birth chart. The moon's position at birth fixes one of the 27 nakshatras, and each nakshatra is associated with a set of starting syllables; a name beginning with one of them is considered auspicious. Practice varies by region and family, so ask your family priest or consult a panchang rather than relying on a generic online table.

Alongside these traditions sits plain personal taste: the sound of a name with the family surname, how grandparents will say it, and how it will work at school in another country.

sections.title: Names of deities and their epithets
sections.content: Naming a son after a god, or after one of a god's epithets, places the child under that deity's blessing and gives him a name with a story. Krishna and his titles are covered in depth in our separate guide, as are the names of Shiva; here are the deity names most widely used.

sections.title: Modern favourites — and what they really mean
sections.content:
A new generation of names has become popular in Indian cities and the diaspora over the last twenty years: Aarav, Vihaan, Vivaan, Reyansh, Kiaan and others. Some have solid Sanskrit roots; others are recent coinages whose meanings are given differently on every website. That does not make them bad names, but it is worth knowing which is which.

Aarav is a good example. It is usually translated as "peaceful" or "calm", yet in classical Sanskrit dictionaries ārava means "sound" or "cry". Vihaan is generally explained as "dawn" or "morning", a sense also given for the Sanskrit word vihāna. Vivaan, Reyansh and Kiaan are modern names whose meanings vary between sources; if the meaning matters to you, choose a name you can trace in a dictionary such as Monier-Williams, available free through the Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries.

sections.title: Regional customs and spelling
sections.content:
India's naming customs differ by region, and they affect how a name appears on documents. In Maharashtra and Gujarat, the father's name traditionally follows the child's given name. Many South Indian families use the father's name or village name as an initial before or after the given name, and some have no family surname at all. Gujarati and Marathi usage adds honorifics such as -bhai and -rao in everyday speech, but these are not part of the registered name.

Spelling is a separate decision. Sanskrit long vowels are written in several ways — Aarav or Arav, Ishaan or Ishan — and some families add or double letters for numerological reasons. Whatever you choose, use one spelling consistently, especially if the child will hold documents in more than one country.

Check how the name reads with your surname and initials.
If you follow nakshatra syllables, confirm them with your family priest.
Look up the meaning in a Sanskrit dictionary if a website's meaning seems vague.

faqs.q: When is the Hindu naming ceremony held?
faqs.a: Traditionally on the tenth or twelfth day after birth, according to the Grihya Sutras. In practice families hold the Namakarana anywhere from about the eleventh day to the child's first birthday.

faqs.q: What does Aarav mean?
faqs.a: Aarav is usually translated as "peaceful" or "calm", but in classical Sanskrit dictionaries ārava means "sound" or "cry". It is a popular modern name; if the meaning matters, be aware of the difference.

faqs.q: How do I find my baby's name letter by nakshatra?
faqs.a: The nakshatra is calculated from the moon's position at the exact time and place of birth, and each nakshatra quarter is associated with a starting syllable. Ask a family priest or use a reliable panchang, as tables vary by tradition.

faqs.q: Is it okay to name a baby after a Hindu god?
faqs.a: Yes. Names of deities and their epithets are among the most traditional Hindu names. Some families prefer an epithet, such as Madhav for Krishna or Shankar for Shiva, over the deity's main name.

faqs.q: Are names like Kabir and Sahil Hindu names?
faqs.a: Kabir and Sahil are of Arabic or Persian origin but are widely used in Hindu families in India; Kabir also honours the poet-saint Kabir, revered across religious traditions.

content.introduction:
Hindu girls' names are among the most lyrical in any language. Sanskrit gives parents words for every shade of light, every river and flower, and every quality from wisdom to grace; the epics and devotional poetry add heroines and saints; and the many names of the goddesses offer hundreds more.

This guide covers Hindu girl names grouped by theme — virtues, light and nature, rivers, heroines and saints — with the meaning most commonly recorded. Goddess names have their own detailed guide. We also explain the classical advice on girls' names, which may surprise you, and flag modern favourites whose meanings are uncertain.
keyTakeaways: Classical texts suggested girls' names with an odd number of syllables, ending in a long ā or ī.
Virtue names such as Ananya, Kavya, Shreya and Vidya remain consistently popular.
Rivers (Ganga, Yamuna, Kaveri), flowers (Padma, Juhi) and light (Jyoti, Diya, Prabha) are classic themes.
Some fashionable names — Kiara, Myra — are not Sanskrit; that is fine, but know where a name comes from.

sections.title: What the classical texts say about girls' names
sections.content:
The Grihya Sutras, which describe the Namakarana ceremony held on the tenth or twelfth day after birth, give specific advice for girls: a name with an odd number of syllables, ending in a long ā or ī, pleasant and easy to pronounce. That pattern is visible in a huge number of Hindu girls' names — Sita, Radha, Gauri, Lakshmi, Savitri. Names connected with a deity, a virtue, a lucky star or beautiful things in nature were recommended; harsh or inauspicious words were to be avoided.

Few families follow the syllable rule strictly today, but many still consider the baby's birth nakshatra, which suggests auspicious starting syllables. Others simply choose a name whose meaning and sound they love. All three approaches are well within tradition.

sections.title: Sanskrit virtue names
sections.content: These names describe a quality or a blessing. They are popular across India and the diaspora because they are meaningful without being tied to one deity, and most are easy to pronounce in English.

content.introduction:
Few figures have given parents as many names as Krishna. Worshipped as the eighth avatar of Vishnu — and in several traditions as the Supreme God himself — he appears as a mischievous child, a cowherd, a lover, a king, a friend and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gita. Each role produced epithets, and devotional tradition gathered them into lists of 108 names and more.

Many of those epithets are now everyday Indian names: Madhav, Keshav, Govind, Gopal, Mohan, Hari, Mukund. This guide explains 35 of them, drawing on standard translations of the Sanskrit titles, and notes which are common today and which are rarer or more formal. It also lists names from Krishna's story for families who want a connection without using one of his own names.
keyTakeaways: Krishna means "dark" or "black" in Sanskrit; devotional traditions also interpret it as "all-attractive".
Popular everyday names include Madhav, Keshav, Govind, Gopal, Mohan, Hari, Mukund and Shyam.
Many epithets come from stories: Damodar (the rope tied round his waist), Giridhar (lifting a mountain), Murari (slayer of Mura).
Names from his circle — Balram, Uddhav, Sudama, and for girls Radha and Rukmini — offer a connection to Krishna's story.

sections.title: Who Krishna is, and why he has so many names
sections.content:
In Hindu tradition Krishna is the eighth avatar of Vishnu, born in Mathura and raised among cowherds in Gokul and Vrindavan. His childhood exploits — stealing butter, lifting Mount Govardhan to shelter the villagers, dancing with the gopis — fill the Bhagavata Purana. As an adult he is the king of Dwarka and the charioteer of Arjuna, to whom he speaks the Bhagavad Gita on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.

Each of these stories produced a title. Some describe his appearance (Shyam, dark; Keshav, with beautiful hair), some his deeds (Giridhar, Murari, Madhusudan), some his relationships (Nandakumar, son of Nanda; Parthasarathi, Arjuna's charioteer) and some his divinity (Achyut, the infallible; Jagannath, lord of the universe). The Vishnu Sahasranama, the thousand names of Vishnu, includes many of them.

sections.title: Names from Krishna's circle

If you want a name connected with Krishna without using one of his own titles, his family, friends and devotees offer good options. For boys: Balram (Balarama), his elder brother, renowned for strength; Uddhav, his friend and counsellor; Sudama, the poor childhood friend whose story is a lesson in devotion; and Nanda and Vasudev, his foster and birth fathers.

For girls, Radha is the most beloved name associated with Krishna, together with Rukmini, his chief queen; Satyabhama, another of his queens; Kalindi, a name of the Yamuna river; Vrinda, the holy basil and the forest of Vrindavan; and Meera, after the poet-saint Mirabai. Yashoda, his foster mother, and Devaki, his birth mother, are honoured names too.

sections.title: Choosing among Krishna's names
sections.content:
With so many names available, a few practical questions help. How formal is the name? Madhav, Keshav and Mohan sit easily in a modern classroom; Parthasarathi and Madhusudan are magnificent but long. Does the story suit a baby? Many families prefer titles of love and protection (Govind, Gopal, Mukund) to titles of combat. And how will it sound with your surname and in the languages your family speaks?

Some families combine a Krishna name with the nakshatra syllable suggested by the baby's birth chart. Others choose the epithet connected with the family's own devotional tradition — Jagannath in Odisha, Vitthal (Vithoba) in Maharashtra, Shrinath in Rajasthan.

content.introduction:
In Hindu tradition the Divine Feminine appears in many forms: Lakshmi, who brings prosperity and grace; Saraswati, goddess of learning, music and speech; Parvati, the mountain's daughter and Shiva's consort; and Durga, the invincible warrior mother, together with her many fierce and gentle forms. Each has hundreds of names in devotional hymns, and a great many of them are given to baby girls.

This guide gathers the most widely used names of the four great goddesses, plus a few other goddess names, with the meaning of each. It also discusses a question many families ask: whether to choose names of the goddesses' fierce forms.
keyTakeaways: Lakshmi names centre on fortune and the lotus: Shree, Padma, Kamala, Indira, Haripriya.
Saraswati names centre on speech, music and whiteness: Vani, Sharada, Bharati, Veena, Shweta.
Parvati names refer to the mountain: Girija, Shailaja, Haimavati — alongside Uma, Gauri and Aparna.
Durga names range from protective (Ambika, Jaya) to fierce (Kali, Chandika); many families prefer the gentler forms for a baby.

sections.title: Names of Lakshmi
sections.content: Lakshmi is the goddess of prosperity, good fortune and beauty, the consort of Vishnu, and is worshipped especially at Diwali. She is traditionally born from the churning of the ocean and is shown seated on a lotus, which is why so many of her names mean lotus. The word lakshmi itself means a sign or mark — specifically an auspicious one — and came to mean good fortune.

sections.title: Names of Saraswati
sections.content: Saraswati is the goddess of knowledge, music, art and speech. Originally a sacred river praised in the Rig Veda, she is depicted dressed in white, holding a veena and seated on a swan or lotus. Students pray to her before exams, and Vasant Panchami is her festival. Her names suit families who value learning and the arts.

names.name: Saraswati
names.meaning: She who possesses flowing waters; goddess of learning

sections.title: Names of Parvati
sections.content: Parvati, "daughter of the mountain", is the consort of Shiva and mother of Ganesha and Kartikeya. Many of her names refer to her father Himavat, the Himalaya; others recall her devotion — Aparna, "leafless", remembers the penance in which she fasted even from leaves to win Shiva. Uma and Gauri are among the oldest and most popular of all Hindu girls' names.

sections.title: Names of Durga
sections.content: Durga, "the invincible" or "the one difficult to approach", is the warrior goddess who defeats the buffalo demon Mahishasura, celebrated during Navaratri and Durga Puja. She is both fierce protector and loving mother, and her names reflect both sides. The gentler names below are widely given to girls.

sections.title: Fierce forms: should you use them?
sections.content:
Some goddess names belong to fierce forms — Kali, Chandika, Chamunda, Bhairavi. These are revered names, and in Bengal and elsewhere Kali in particular is used, but many families prefer not to give a baby the name of a goddess's most terrifying form. Some also feel a name such as Durga or Kali carries expectations a child must live up to.

There is no single rule. A useful compromise is to choose a gentle name of the same goddess: Ambika or Jaya for Durga, Gauri or Uma for Parvati. If you are unsure, your family priest or elders can tell you what is customary in your community.

faqs.q: What are the best names of Goddess Lakshmi for a baby girl?
faqs.a: Popular Lakshmi names include Shree, Padma, Kamala, Indira, Haripriya, Vaishnavi and Lakshmi itself — most connected with good fortune or the lotus.

faqs.q: What are Saraswati names for a girl?
faqs.a: Vani (speech), Sharada, Bharati, Veena, Vidya (knowledge), Medha (intelligence), Shweta (white) and Hamsini (she who rides a swan) are well-loved Saraswati names.

faqs.q: Is it okay to name a baby Durga or Kali?
faqs.a: Both are revered names and are used, but many families prefer gentler names of the same goddess — Ambika or Jaya for Durga — for a baby. It depends on your family's custom.

faqs.q: What does Aparna mean?
faqs.a: Aparna means "leafless". It is a name of Parvati, recalling the penance in which she fasted even from leaves to win Shiva as her husband.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Uma and Gauri?
faqs.a: Both are names of Parvati. Gauri means fair or radiant; Uma is one of her most ancient names and is often glossed as light or tranquillity.

content.introduction:
Shiva — Mahadev, the Great God — is worshipped across India and beyond as the destroyer and transformer in the Hindu trinity, the ascetic of Mount Kailash, the cosmic dancer and the gentle husband of Parvati. Like Krishna, he is known by a great many names, collected in hymns such as the Shiva Sahasranama, and dozens of them have become everyday Indian names.

This guide explains the most popular names of Shiva, groups them by the stories they come from, and adds a set of names drawn from the twelve Jyotirlingas, Shiva's most sacred temples. Meanings follow the standard Sanskrit sense of each title.
keyTakeaways: Shiva means "auspicious" or "kind" in Sanskrit; Shankar means "bestower of welfare".
Neelkanth (blue-throated) recalls Shiva drinking the poison from the churning of the ocean.
Ashutosh — "easily pleased" — is one of the most popular modern names of Shiva.
The twelve Jyotirlingas give names such as Somnath, Kedar, Vishwanath, Omkar and Rameshwar.

sections.title: Names from Shiva's stories and form
sections.content: Many of Shiva's names describe his appearance or recall famous episodes. Neelkanth remembers the churning of the ocean (Samudra Manthan), when a deadly poison, halahala, rose from the waters and Shiva drank it to save the world; Parvati held his throat so it would not descend, and it turned blue. Gangadhar recalls how he caught the river Ganga in his matted locks as she descended from heaven, so her force would not shatter the earth.

sections.title: Names from the twelve Jyotirlingas
sections.content: The Jyotirlingas are twelve shrines where Shiva is believed to have manifested as a column of light, and pilgrimage to them is one of the great journeys of Hindu devotion. Several of their names have become given names, especially for children born to families devoted to a particular temple. (The locations of a few, such as Vaidyanath and Nageshwar, are claimed by more than one temple; we give the most commonly cited site.)

sections.title: Gentle or fierce?
sections.content:
Shiva has peaceful and terrifying aspects, and his names reflect both. Bhairav and Mahakal belong to his fierce forms, and while both are used as names, some families prefer a gentler title for a baby. Ashutosh, Shankar, Shambhu, Bholenath and Umapati speak of his kindness, his ease of being pleased and his family life, which is why they are perennial favourites.

Shiva's family also offers names: his sons Ganesh and Kartikeya (also called Skanda, Murugan and Subramanya in the South), and for girls the many names of Parvati, which are covered in our guide to goddess names.

sections.title: Choosing a Shiva name for your son
sections.content:
Start with the feel you want. For a short, modern name, Shiv, Ishaan, Rudra, Kedar and Omkar all work well in any setting. For a traditional name with devotional weight, Shankar, Mahesh, Ashutosh and Gangadhar are timeless. If your family has a connection to a particular temple or pilgrimage, a Jyotirlinga name can carry that story for life.

As with any name, say it with your surname, check how it will be spelled and pronounced in the countries where your child will live, and ask elders whether there are family customs to respect — for example, not repeating the name of a living relative.

Gentle and devotional: Ashutosh, Shankar, Shambhu, Umapati, Bholenath.

faqs.q: What does Shiva mean?

faqs.q: Why is Shiva called Neelkanth?
faqs.a: During the churning of the ocean, a deadly poison rose from the waters. Shiva drank it to protect the world, and Parvati stopped it in his throat, which turned blue — hence Neelkanth, "the blue-throated one".

faqs.q: What does Ashutosh mean?
faqs.a: Ashutosh means "one who is easily pleased", referring to Shiva's readiness to grant his devotees' wishes. It is a popular boys' name.

faqs.q: What are the twelve Jyotirlingas?

sections.title: How to read a biblical name
sections.content:
Most Old Testament names are Hebrew sentences in miniature. A large share are theophoric, containing a name of God: El (as in Daniel, "God is my judge", or Gabriel, "God is my strength") or a short form of Yahweh, written -iah, -jah or Jo- in English (Elijah, "my God is Yahweh"; Isaiah, "Yahweh is salvation"; Jonathan, "Yahweh has given"). Others commemorate the circumstances of birth: Genesis explains Isaac ("he laughs") through Sarah's laughter and Benjamin ("son of the right hand") through Jacob renaming the child Rachel had called Ben-oni, "son of my sorrow".

New Testament names are more mixed: Hebrew and Aramaic names (John, Thomas, Matthew), Greek names (Andrew, Philip, Stephen, Timothy) and Latin names (Paul, Mark, Titus). Bible Gateway lets you search any name across many translations if you want to read every passage where it occurs.

The Bible is honest about its villains, and a handful of names are rarely chosen because of the stories attached to them: Cain, who killed his brother; Judas, who betrayed Jesus; Ahab, the idolatrous king. Others carry mixed associations — Absalom rebelled against his father David, and Esau sold his birthright. None of this is a rule, and some of these names are used, but it is worth reading a figure's story before you commit.

It is also worth checking how a name has been used more recently. A biblical name can pick up modern associations — a celebrity, a fictional character — that matter in your community.
