keyTakeaways: Elizabeth (No. 17 for 2025 births) is the highest-ranked biblical girl name in SSA's top 20.
Several famous names have debated meanings: Mary, Rebecca, Ruth and Leah among them.
Lesser-known names such as Tirzah, Keziah, Jemima and Junia have strong stories.
Grace, Faith and Hope are virtue names: biblical in spirit, not names of biblical women.

sections.title: Women of the Old Testament
sections.content: The matriarchs of Genesis, the heroines of Judges and Ruth, and the queen of the Book of Esther give the best-known Hebrew girls' names. Read their stories before choosing — several are more complex than the name's gentle sound suggests.

names.name: Sarah
names.note: Wife of Abraham, renamed from Sarai (Genesis 17:15)

names.name: Rebecca
names.meaning: Debated; often linked to "to tie, bind"

names.name: Esther
names.meaning: Probably Persian "star"; her Hebrew name was Hadassah, "myrtle"

names.name: Tamar
names.note: Several women; their stories are difficult

sections.title: Lesser-known Old Testament gems
sections.content: If you want a biblical name that few classmates will share, look at the minor figures. Job's three daughters, born after his trials, are named in Job 42:14 — Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch — and the five daughters of Zelophehad (Numbers 27) famously won the right to inherit their father's land.

names.name: Noa
names.meaning: Movement — a different name from Noah

names.name: Elisheba
names.meaning: My God is an oath — the Hebrew root of Elizabeth

sections.title: Women of the New Testament
sections.content: The Gospels and Acts introduce Mary the mother of Jesus, Mary Magdalene, the sisters Martha and Mary of Bethany, and the women who led and supported the first Christian communities. Several of these names are Greek or Latin, reflecting the world of the early church.

names.name: Mary
names.meaning: From Miriam; meaning debated ("beloved", "bitter", "wished-for child" are all proposed)

names.name: Elizabeth
names.note: Mother of John the Baptist; No. 17 for 2025 births

sections.title: Virtue names: biblical in spirit
sections.content: Grace, Faith, Hope, Charity, Mercy, Joy and Patience became given names in England after the Reformation, when Puritan families looked for names expressing Christian virtues. They are not names of women in the Bible, but they come straight from its language — "faith, hope and love" (1 Corinthians 13:13) — and Grace in particular has remained a steady favourite. If a name's biblical credentials matter to you, it is worth knowing the difference.

sections.title: Names with complicated stories
sections.content:
Some biblical names are lovely to say and difficult to read about. Delilah betrayed Samson to the Philistines (Judges 16), yet the name is in BabyCenter's 2026 top 40 — for many parents its sound now outweighs its story. Jezebel, the queen who persecuted the prophets, is almost never used. Tamar's stories involve abuse, and Bathsheba's begins with David's wrongdoing.

None of this need rule a name out; it is simply worth knowing what a name will remind some people of. Reading the passage on Bible Gateway takes a few minutes and avoids surprises.

faqs.q: What are the most popular biblical girl names?
faqs.a: Elizabeth is No. 17 in SSA's ranking for girls born in 2025. Other long-popular biblical names include Hannah, Abigail, Sarah, Leah, Naomi, Lydia and Anna, and BabyCenter's in-progress 2026 table includes Delilah.

faqs.q: What does Mary mean?
faqs.a: Mary comes from the Hebrew Miriam, whose meaning is debated. Proposed meanings include "beloved" (possibly from Egyptian), "bitter" and "wished-for child".

faqs.q: Is Grace a biblical name?
faqs.a: Grace is a virtue name taken from biblical language, adopted by Puritan families after the Reformation. It is not the name of a woman in the Bible.

faqs.q: Are Noa and Noah the same name?
faqs.a: No. In Hebrew, Noah (Noach) means "rest", while Noa (No'ah), one of the daughters of Zelophehad in Numbers 27, means "movement". They are spelled differently in Hebrew.

faqs.q: What are rare biblical girl names?
faqs.a: Tirzah, Keziah, Jemima, Milcah, Adah, Junia, Eunice and Elisheba are established biblical names that are far less common than Sarah or Hannah.

title: Saint Names for Baby Boys and Girls: Patron Saints, Feast Days and Meanings
seoTitle: Saint Names for Baby Boys and Girls (Feast Days)
subtitle: Popular Catholic and Christian saint names with their meanings, feast days and what each saint is patron of.
excerpt: Saint names for babies with meanings and feast days — Francis, Anthony, Patrick, Teresa, Clare, Lucy, Cecilia and more — plus name days and confirmation names.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Naming a child after a saint gives them more than a name: a patron, a story of faith and, in many Catholic and Orthodox families, a feast day to celebrate alongside their birthday. The custom is ancient and still strong. Many families choose a saint whose feast falls near the baby's birth, a saint connected with the family's heritage, or simply a saint whose life they admire.

This guide lists popular saint names for boys and girls with each name's meaning, the saint's feast day and what the saint is traditionally patron of. Feast days follow the General Roman Calendar unless noted; some saints are celebrated on different dates in national calendars or in the Orthodox churches.
keyTakeaways: Many Catholic and Orthodox families celebrate a child's name day — the feast of their patron saint.
Feast dates here follow the General Roman Calendar; national and Orthodox calendars can differ.
Gianna — after St Gianna Beretta Molla — is in BabyCenter's 2026 top 40 for girls.
Catholics often take a second saint's name at confirmation, so a baptismal name need not be a saint's.

sections.title: Why families choose saint names
sections.content:
In the early church, converts often took the name of an apostle or martyr, and by the Middle Ages most European children were named after saints. The Catholic Church's Code of Canon Law asks only that a name not be "foreign to Christian sensibility"; a saint's name is encouraged but not required. Many Catholics also choose a confirmation name — a saint they adopt as an additional patron in their teens.

In Orthodox countries such as Greece, and in parts of Catholic Europe and Latin America, a person's name day (the feast of their saint) can be celebrated as much as a birthday. Choosing a saint whose feast is close to the baby's birthday is a popular way of linking the two.

sections.title: Saint names for boys
sections.content: These saints are among the most widely honoured in the Western church, and their names remain common in many languages.

names.name: Francis
names.note: Francis of Assisi — 4 October; animals and ecology

names.name: Anthony
names.meaning: From the Roman family name Antonius
names.note: Anthony of Padua — 13 June; lost things

names.name: Joseph
names.note: 19 March (and 1 May, Joseph the Worker); fathers, workers

names.name: Ignatius
names.meaning: From the Roman name Egnatius; associated with ignis, fire

names.name: Christopher
names.note: 25 July; travellers (now a local rather than universal feast)

sections.title: Saint names for girls
sections.content: Women saints include martyrs of the early church, mystics and doctors of the church, founders of religious orders and modern saints canonised in living memory. Gianna, after St Gianna Beretta Molla (canonised in 2004), is now in BabyCenter's in-progress 2026 top 40 for girls.

names.name: Cecilia
names.meaning: From the Roman family name Caecilius

sections.title: The apostles and evangelists
sections.content:
The twelve apostles and the four evangelists are the foundation of Christian naming. Their feasts are fixed in the universal calendar: Andrew on 30 November, John on 27 December, Matthew on 21 September, Luke on 18 October, Mark on 25 April, Peter and Paul together on 29 June, Thomas on 3 July, James the Greater on 25 July, Bartholomew on 24 August, and Simon and Jude together on 28 October. Stephen, the first martyr, is remembered on 26 December.

These names are so familiar that parents sometimes forget they are saints' names at all — which is part of their appeal: they work in any setting and in almost any language.

sections.title: Choosing a patron saint for your child
sections.content:
There is no single right way to choose. Some families look up the saints whose feast falls on or near the birthday; others choose a saint linked to a parent's profession, the family's country of origin, or a cause close to their hearts. Patronages are traditional associations — Anthony for lost things, Cecilia for music, Jude for desperate causes — rather than official appointments, and they vary between countries.

If you want an unusual saint's name, national calendars and the lives of modern saints are rich sources: Zélie (Zélie Martin, mother of Thérèse), Kateri, Gianna, Faustina and Maximilian have all been canonised in recent decades.
bullets: Check the feast date in your own country's calendar, which may differ from the universal one.
Read a short life of the saint — the story is part of the name.
Consider how the name works in the languages your family speaks.
Remember a confirmation name can add a second patron later.

faqs.q: Do Catholic babies have to be named after a saint?
faqs.a: No. Canon law asks that a name not be foreign to Christian sensibility. A saint's name is encouraged, and many Catholics add a saint's name at confirmation.

faqs.q: What is a name day?
faqs.a: A name day is the feast day of the saint whose name a person bears. In Greece and other Orthodox countries, and in parts of Catholic Europe and Latin America, name days are widely celebrated.

faqs.q: Which saint names are popular today?
faqs.a: Many saint names remain common, including Joseph, Thomas, Francis, Nicholas, Sebastian, Lucy, Clare and Josephine. Gianna, after St Gianna Beretta Molla, is in BabyCenter's in-progress 2026 top 40 for girls.

faqs.q: How do I find my baby's patron saint?
faqs.a: Look up the saints whose feasts fall on or near the birthday in your national liturgical calendar, or choose a saint whose life or patronage is meaningful to your family.

faqs.q: Are feast days the same everywhere?
faqs.a: Not always. The General Roman Calendar sets universal dates, but national calendars add or move some feasts, and the Orthodox churches follow their own calendars.

title: How to Choose a Baby Name: A Step-by-Step Guide for Parents
seoTitle: How to Choose a Baby Name: 10-Step Guide
subtitle: A practical, culture-aware process — from a long list to a name you are sure of — with checks most guides skip.
excerpt: How to choose a baby name in 10 steps: build a long list, check meaning and popularity with real data, test sound and spelling, and decide together.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide
tags: how to choose a baby name
seoKeywords: how to choose a baby name
how to pick a baby name

content.introduction:
Choosing a baby name is one of the first big decisions parents make together, and it can be surprisingly hard. There are tens of thousands of possible names, everyone has an opinion, and the choice feels permanent — because it largely is.

This guide sets out a practical process in ten steps. It starts with what matters to your family, moves through a long list and a short list, and adds the checks that prevent regret: confirming a name's real meaning, looking at genuine popularity data rather than impressions, testing the full name aloud, and thinking about spelling, initials and cultural or religious customs. Use as many of the steps as help you.
keyTakeaways: Agree your priorities first — heritage, faith, meaning, sound, uniqueness — before collecting names.
Check meanings in more than one source; popular name lists often repeat unsupported meanings.
Use real data for popularity: SSA's top 1,000 covered about 72% of US babies born in 2025.
Test the full name aloud, check initials and nicknames, and pick one spelling.
Live with a shortlist for a while before deciding, and agree how you will settle disagreements.

sections.title: Step 1: Decide what matters to you
sections.content:
Before you look at a single list, talk about priorities. Is it important that the name reflects your heritage or faith? Do you want to honour a relative? Does the meaning matter more than the sound? Would you prefer a familiar name or a rare one? Do you want a name that works in two languages?

Writing down three or four priorities — and noticing where you and your partner differ — saves a great deal of circular debate later. It also gives you a way to judge names: a beautiful name that fails your top priority is probably not the one.

sections.title: Step 2: Build a long list
sections.content:
Gather candidates generously at this stage; you will cut later. Good sources include your family tree, your religious tradition's scripture and saints, the languages your family speaks, literature and history, and names with meanings you love. Name sites and books are useful for ideas, but treat their meanings as starting points.

Browsing by theme often works better than scrolling alphabetical lists: names that mean light or strength, biblical names, Quranic names, Sanskrit names of deities. Aim for twenty to fifty names you both find at least interesting.
bullets: Family names, including surnames from either side that could work as first names.
Scripture, saints, prophets or deities from your tradition.
Words with meanings that matter to you, in the languages you speak.
Names of people you admire — from history, literature or your own life.

sections.title: Step 3: Check the meaning properly
sections.content:
A name's meaning is something your child may explain for the rest of their life, so it is worth getting right. Look each finalist up in at least two independent references — an etymological dictionary such as Behind the Name, a scripture search, or a language dictionary — and be wary of meanings that appear only on name lists.

Three things commonly go wrong. Popular sites sometimes give flattering meanings that the original language does not support. Some names have debated etymologies, and a single confident meaning hides that. And a name can mean something unfortunate in another language your family or community speaks. A few minutes of checking prevents all three.

sections.title: Step 4: Look at real popularity data
sections.content:
Impressions of popularity are often wrong — a name can feel everywhere because it is fashionable in your circle, or feel rare when it is in fact common nationally. Use real data. In the US, the Social Security Administration publishes the top 1,000 names for each birth year, with counts, and state-level rankings; the newest data covers babies born in 2025.

Two facts help put the numbers in perspective. Even the No. 1 name, Liam, was given to about one boy in a hundred born in 2025. And the entire top 1,000 covered only about 72% of babies that year, according to SSA, so names outside the top 1,000 are genuinely uncommon. Decide what you want: a familiar name, or one your child is unlikely to share with a classmate.
bullets: Check national rank and count for the latest year.
Check your state or region — local tastes differ a lot.
Look at the trend over several years, not just one.
Remember spelling variants are counted separately.

sections.title: Step 5: Say the full name aloud
sections.content:
Write and say the full name — first, middle and family name — many times. Listen for rhythm: names often flow well when the number of syllables varies between first and last name. Listen for awkward runs of sound, such as a first name ending with the sound the surname begins with. Check that the name does not rhyme comically with the surname.

Then look at the initials and the obvious nicknames. Initials that spell an unfortunate word, and nicknames you would not want your child called, are easier to spot now than at school. Finally, imagine the name at every age: on a baby, a teenager, a job application and a grandparent.

sections.title: Step 6: Choose one spelling and test pronunciation
sections.content:
Many names have several spellings, especially names transliterated from Arabic, Hebrew, Sanskrit or other scripts. Choose the spelling that matches how your family says the name, and use it identically on the birth certificate, passport and every other document; mismatched spellings can cause real administrative trouble.

Test the name on a few people who do not know it: can they read it correctly, and spell it after hearing it? A name that is regularly misread is perfectly usable, but your child will spend time correcting it — a cost worth weighing honestly against the name's appeal.

sections.title: Step 7: Respect cultural and religious customs
sections.content:
Many traditions have customs around naming that affect both the choice and the timing. Hindu families traditionally hold the Namakarana on the tenth or twelfth day after birth and may choose a starting syllable from the baby's birth star. Muslim families often name the baby on the day of birth or on the seventh day, together with the aqiqah. In the Sikh Naam Karan, the first letter of the name traditionally comes from a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib opened at random. Jewish boys are usually named at the brit milah on the eighth day, and many Ashkenazi families avoid naming a child after a living relative. Catholic families often choose a saint's name.

If your family includes more than one tradition, look for names that work in both, or use first and middle names to honour each.

sections.title: Step 8: Check the practical and legal side
sections.content:
Registration rules vary by country and state. Most places set a deadline for registering a birth, and some limit what a name can contain — for example, numerals, symbols or very long names may be rejected. A few countries, such as Iceland and Denmark, maintain official lists of approved names, and others allow registrars to refuse names considered harmful to the child.

It is also worth a quick internet search of the full name, to make sure it is not strongly associated with a well-known person or brand you would rather avoid.

sections.title: Step 9: Live with your shortlist
sections.content:
Narrow your list to three to five names, then live with them. Use each name for a few days — say it to the bump, write it down, imagine introducing your child. Many parents find one name starts to feel right while another quietly drops away.

Decide in advance how much to share. Telling a few trusted people can be helpful; announcing a shortlist to the whole family often invites lobbying. Some parents keep the name private until the baby is born, which also leaves room to change your mind when you meet them.
bullets: Save your favourites to a shortlist so you can compare them side by side.
Revisit the list after a week; notice which names you keep coming back to.
Ask one or two trusted people for honest reactions, not votes.

sections.title: Step 10: Decide together
sections.content:
Disagreement is normal. Simple rules help: each partner can veto any name without needing to justify it; names that survive go on the shared list; and you rank the shortlist separately before comparing. Some couples agree that one parent chooses the first name and the other the middle name.

When you have a name you both feel good about — one that meets your priorities, has a meaning you have checked, sounds right with your family name and works in your community — you can stop. There is no perfect name, only one that is right for your child and your family.

faqs.q: When should we start choosing a baby name?
faqs.a: Many parents start in the second trimester and settle on a shortlist before the birth, leaving the final decision until they meet the baby. Check your local deadline for registering the birth so you know how much time you have.

faqs.q: How can we agree on a name?
faqs.a: Agree your priorities first, give each partner a veto, build a shared list of names that survive, and rank the shortlist separately before comparing. Some couples split first and middle names.

faqs.q: Is it bad to choose a popular name?
faqs.a: No. A popular name is familiar and easy to spell. Check the real data: even the No. 1 US name, Liam, was given to about one boy in a hundred born in 2025.

faqs.q: How do we check how rare a name is?
faqs.a: In the US, look the name up in Social Security Administration data for the latest birth year. The top 1,000 names covered about 72% of babies born in 2025, so names outside it are genuinely uncommon.

faqs.q: Should we tell family the name before the birth?
faqs.a: It is a personal choice. Sharing with a few trusted people can be useful, but announcing a shortlist widely often invites lobbying. Many parents keep the final name private until the baby arrives.

title: Baby Names That Mean Light: 60 Radiant Names from Every Tradition
seoTitle: Baby Names That Mean Light (Boys & Girls)
subtitle: Names meaning light, brightness, lamp, dawn and sun — in Arabic, Sanskrit, Hebrew, Latin, Greek, Persian and more.
excerpt: Baby names that mean light for boys and girls: Noor, Lucy, Jyoti, Uriel, Roshan, Clara, Ziya, Prakash and more — with meanings checked and myths flagged.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Light is one of the oldest and most universal images in naming. It stands for knowledge, goodness, hope and the divine in almost every tradition: "God is the Light of the heavens and the earth" in the Quran (24:35), "I am the light of the world" in the Gospel of John (8:12), and the lamps of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights. Unsurprisingly, every language has given parents names that mean light, brightness or a lamp.

This guide gathers 60 of them by language, with the meaning of each. We also flag a few names that are often listed as meaning "light" but do not — Lucas is the best-known example — so that you can choose with confidence.
keyTakeaways: Arabic gives Noor, Nura, Munir, Anwar, Siraj and Ziya; Sanskrit gives Jyoti, Prakash, Deepak, Kiran and Tejas.
Hebrew light names include Uri, Uriel, Ora, Liora, Meir and Neriah.
Lucy, Lucia and Lucian come from Latin lux, light — but Lucas originally meant "man from Lucania".
Clara, Phoebe and Roshan mean bright; Aurora and Usha mean dawn.

sections.title: Arabic and Islamic names meaning light
sections.content: Light (nur) is one of the richest words in the Quran. Surah 24 is named an-Nur, and its Verse of Light is among the most famous passages in Islamic scripture; the Prophet is described in 33:46 as "a luminous lamp" (sirajan munira). Many Muslim names grow from these words.

names.name: Noor
names.note: Used for girls and boys; also Nur

sections.title: Sanskrit and Hindu names meaning light
sections.content: Hindu tradition celebrates light in the festival of Diwali and in prayers such as "tamaso mā jyotir gamaya" — "lead me from darkness to light" (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad). Sanskrit has dozens of words for light, flame, ray and radiance, and many are popular names.

sections.title: Hebrew and biblical names meaning light
sections.content: Hebrew light names are especially popular in Israel and among Jewish families worldwide, and several appear in the Bible. Uriel is one of the archangels of Jewish tradition; Neriah was the father of Baruch, the scribe of Jeremiah.

sections.title: Latin, Greek and European names meaning light
sections.content: Latin lux (light) and lucidus (bright), Greek phos and phoibos, and the Germanic element beraht (bright) are behind many familiar European names. A little care is needed: several popular names are linked to light by folk etymology rather than history.

sections.title: Names meaning dawn and sunrise
sections.content: Dawn — the first light of day — is a theme of its own, with a hopeful, new-beginning feel that suits a baby name.

names.name: Aurora
names.note: No. 15 for US girls born in 2025 (SSA)

sections.title: Names often said to mean light — but don't
sections.content:
Name lists frequently attach "light" to names whose history says otherwise. Lucas, for example, comes from the Greek Loukas, "man from Lucania", a region of southern Italy; it has been associated with lux by sound, not by origin. Helen and Eleanor are often glossed as "light" or "torch", but the etymology of Helen is genuinely uncertain and Eleanor's is debated. Ciara and Kieran mean "dark" or "black-haired" in Irish — the opposite.

None of this makes them poor names. But if the meaning "light" is the reason you are choosing a name, pick one where the meaning is secure: Lucy, Clara, Noor, Jyoti, Uriel and Roshan all qualify.
bullets: Lucas — "man from Lucania", not "light" (though Lucy and Lucia do mean light).
Helen — etymology uncertain; "torch" and "light" are guesses.
Ciara, Kieran — Irish for "dark".
Ayla — Turkish "halo of the moon"; Hebrew "oak", not simply "light".

faqs.q: What girl names mean light?
faqs.a: Girl names that mean light include Noor, Nura, Lucy, Lucia, Jyoti, Prabha, Roshni, Ora, Liora, Clara (bright), Phoebe (radiant) and Svetlana.

faqs.q: What boy names mean light?
faqs.a: Boy names that mean light include Uriel (God is my light), Uri, Meir, Munir, Anwar, Siraj, Prakash, Deepak, Tejas, Kiran, Roshan and Lucian.

faqs.q: Does Lucas mean light?
faqs.a: Not originally. Lucas comes from the Greek Loukas, meaning a man from Lucania in southern Italy. It is often linked to Latin lux (light) because of the sound, but Lucy and Lucia are the names that genuinely come from lux.

faqs.q: What Islamic names mean light?
faqs.a: Noor, Nura, Munir, Munira, Anwar, Siraj, Ziya and Nuruddin are Islamic names connected with light. The Quran's Surah 24 is called an-Nur, "The Light".

faqs.q: What Hindu names mean light?
faqs.a: Jyoti, Prakash, Deepak, Deepa, Diya, Kiran, Tejas, Prabha and Ujjwal are Hindu names meaning light, lamp, ray or brilliance.

title: Baby Names That Mean Strength: Strong Names for Boys and Girls
seoTitle: Baby Names That Mean Strength (Boys & Girls)
subtitle: Names meaning strength, power, courage and lion — from Hebrew, Arabic, Sanskrit, Latin and Germanic roots.
excerpt: Baby names that mean strength for boys and girls: Ethan, Gabriel, Hamza, Shaurya, Valentina, Audrey, Matilda and more, with their real meanings.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Parents choosing a strong name are usually after more than muscle. Across languages, names that mean strength also carry ideas of steadfastness, courage, protection and faith — "God is my strength" is one of the oldest name meanings in the world.

This guide collects names meaning strength, power, bravery and "lion" from Hebrew, Arabic, Sanskrit, Latin, Greek and Germanic traditions, for boys and girls, with the meaning of each. Where a popular gloss stretches the truth, we say so.
keyTakeaways: Ethan (from Eitan) means firm, enduring; Gabriel means "God is my strength".
Valentina, Valerie and Valentine come from Latin valere, to be strong.
Germanic names such as Audrey, Matilda, Richard and Bernard combine elements meaning strength, battle and bravery.
Lion names — Ari, Asad, Haider, Leo, Leonard — are a strength theme of their own.

sections.title: Hebrew and biblical names meaning strength
sections.content: Many Hebrew names express strength as a gift of God. Gabriel, Ezekiel and Uzziel all contain El, a word for God, while Ethan comes from a word for firmness and endurance. Ethan, Gabriel and Ezekiel are all well established in the United States.

names.name: Gabriella
names.meaning: Feminine of Gabriel, "God is my strength"

sections.title: Arabic and Islamic names meaning strength
sections.content: Arabic strength names often come in two families: words for strength and firmness, and words for the lion — a classic image of courage. Haidar ("lion") is a famous title of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin. Some strength words are also divine names: al-Qawi (the Strong) and al-Matin (the Firm) are among the 99 Names, so some families prefer them in Abd- compounds.

sections.title: Sanskrit and Hindu names meaning strength
sections.content: Sanskrit offers many words for valour, vitality and power, and the epics supply strong heroes — Bhima, the mightiest of the Pandavas, and Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, whose name begins with bala, strength. For girls, Shakti (divine power) and Durga (the invincible) are the classic strength names.

sections.title: Latin and Greek names meaning strength
sections.content: Latin valere (to be strong, healthy) gives a whole family of names, and Greek contributes names of courage and protection. Valentina is especially popular in the Americas — it is in BabyCenter's in-progress 2026 top 40 for girls.

names.name: Valerie
names.meaning: From Valerius, from valere, to be strong

names.name: Leo
names.note: No. 19 for US boys born in 2025 (SSA)

sections.title: Germanic names meaning strength and courage
sections.content: Old Germanic names were built from two meaningful elements, and strength, battle and bravery were favourite themes. These names reached English through the Anglo-Saxons and Normans, and many feel classic today.

sections.title: Choosing a strong name that still feels gentle
sections.content:
A strength meaning does not have to come with a hard sound. Gabriel, Ezekiel and Audrey are soft to the ear and strong in meaning; Ojas and Ari are short and gentle. On the other hand, a name like Bhim or Abbas makes its strength obvious. Think about which you want, and say the name with your surname.

It is also worth checking how popular a strong name is where you live. Leo, Gabriel and Ethan are common in the US; Uzziel, Mateen or Ojas are rare. Real data — such as the Social Security Administration's annual rankings — is more reliable than impressions.
bullets: Gentle sound, strong meaning: Gabriel, Audrey, Ezekiel, Ojas, Ari.
Bold sound, strong meaning: Bhim, Abbas, Matilda, Richard, Vikram.
Lion names: Ari, Asad, Haider, Abbas, Leo, Leonard.

faqs.q: What boy names mean strength?
faqs.a: Boy names meaning strength include Ethan (firm), Gabriel (God is my strength), Ezekiel (God strengthens), Hamza, Mateen, Shaurya (valour), Veer (brave), Ojas (vitality), Richard (strong ruler) and Alexander (defender).

faqs.q: What girl names mean strength?
faqs.a: Girl names meaning strength include Valentina and Valerie (strong, healthy), Audrey (noble strength), Matilda (might in battle), Gabriella (God is my strength), Shakti (power), Durga (invincible) and Andrea (courage).

faqs.q: Which names mean lion?
faqs.a: Names meaning lion include Ari (Hebrew), Asad and Haider (Arabic), Leo (Latin) and Leonard ("brave as a lion", Germanic). Abbas is also associated with the lion in Arabic.

faqs.q: Does Bridget mean strength?
faqs.a: Bridget comes from the Irish Brighid, usually explained as "exalted one". It is often listed as meaning strength or power, which is a looser gloss.

faqs.q: What does Ethan mean?
faqs.a: Ethan comes from the Hebrew Eitan, meaning firm, strong or enduring. Ethan the Ezrahite is named in the Bible as a wise man (1 Kings 4:31).

title: Baby Names That Mean Gift from God: 45 Names in Every Tradition
seoTitle: Baby Names That Mean Gift from God (Boys & Girls)

content.introduction:
For many parents, especially after a long wait, "gift from God" is exactly what a child is — and many languages have names that say so. Hebrew gives Matthew, Nathaniel and Jonathan; Greek gives Theodore and Dorothy; Arabic gives Ataullah and Hibatullah; Sanskrit gives Devadatta; Slavic languages give Bogdan.

This guide lists names meaning "gift of God", "given by God" or simply "gift", for boys and girls, with the language each comes from. It also separates them from two groups that are often mixed in: names meaning "God is gracious" (John, Hannah) and a few names wrongly listed as "gift of God".
keyTakeaways: Theodore, Theodora, Dorothy and Dorothea all come from Greek theos (God) and doron (gift).
Matthew, Mateo and Matthias mean "gift of Yahweh"; Nathaniel and Jonathan mean "God/Yahweh has given".
Arabic Ataullah and Hibatullah mean "gift of God"; Hiba and Atiya mean "gift".
Isidore means "gift of Isis" — a goddess — and is not a "gift of God" name.

sections.title: Hebrew and biblical names
sections.content: Hebrew has several verbs for giving, and the names built on them are among the most common in the Western world. Theodore and Mateo are a striking pair in the latest US data: in the Social Security Administration's ranking for babies born in 2025, Theodore is No. 4 and Mateo, the Spanish form of Matthew, is No. 8.

names.name: Mateo
names.note: No. 8 for US boys born in 2025

sections.title: Greek and European names
sections.content: Greek theos (God) and doron (gift) combine in both orders — Theodoros and Dorotheos — giving two families of names. Slavic and Latin languages add their own "given by God" names.

names.name: Theodore
names.note: No. 4 for US boys born in 2025

sections.title: Arabic and Islamic names
sections.content: In Arabic, 'ata' and hiba both mean gift, and adding Allah makes "gift of God". Al-Wahhab, "the Bestower", is one of the 99 Names of God, so Abdul-Wahhab ("servant of the Bestower") belongs to the same theme.

sections.title: Sanskrit and Hindu names
sections.content: Sanskrit datta (given) and dāna (gift) appear in many names, often joined to a deity: Devadatta, "given by the gods"; Haridatt, "given by Hari". Prasad — the blessed offering returned to devotees after worship — is a popular name with a similar sense of divine grace.

sections.title: "God is gracious" names: a close cousin
sections.content:
Many lists of "gift from God" names include John, Jane, Joanna, Giovanni, Ivan, Ian and Hannah. These mean something related but different: John (Yohanan) means "Yahweh is gracious", and Hannah means "grace, favour". If grace is the feeling you want, they are wonderful choices — just know they are about God's grace rather than a gift.

The same applies to Ayaan, a popular name often listed online as "gift of God": its origin is uncertain and that meaning is not well attested, so treat it with caution if the meaning matters to you.

sections.title: Names that do not mean gift from God
sections.content:
A few names turn up on "gift of God" lists by mistake. Isidore is the clearest: it comes from Greek Isidoros, "gift of Isis" — an Egyptian goddess — and Isadora is its feminine. Jesse is sometimes glossed as "gift", but the meaning of the Hebrew Yishai is uncertain. Theia and Thea are Greek names connected with the divine but do not include the word for gift.

If the meaning is your reason for choosing a name, the safest choices are those whose roots literally say it: Theodore, Dorothy, Matthew, Nathaniel, Jonathan, Ataullah, Hibatullah, Devadatta and Bogdan.
bullets: Isidore / Isadora — "gift of Isis", not of God.
Jesse — meaning uncertain.
Ayaan — popular, but "gift of God" is not well attested.
John, Hannah — "God is gracious" / "grace", a different meaning.

faqs.q: What boy names mean gift from God?
faqs.a: Boy names meaning gift from God include Matthew, Mateo, Matthias, Theodore, Nathaniel, Jonathan, Elnathan, Zebadiah, Ataullah, Hibatullah, Devadatta and Bogdan.

faqs.q: What girl names mean gift from God?
faqs.a: Girl names meaning gift from God include Theodora, Dorothy, Dorothea, Netanya, Bogdana, Hiba (gift) and Atiya (gift).

faqs.q: Does Theodore mean gift of God?
faqs.a: Yes. Theodore comes from the Greek Theodoros, from theos (God) and doron (gift). It was the No. 4 boys' name for US babies born in 2025, according to the Social Security Administration.

faqs.q: Does Isidore mean gift of God?
faqs.a: No. Isidore comes from the Greek Isidoros, meaning "gift of Isis", the Egyptian goddess.

faqs.q: What Islamic name means gift from God?
faqs.a: Ataullah and Hibatullah both mean "gift of God" in Arabic, and Hiba and Atiya mean "gift". Khudadad is a Persian name meaning "given by God".

content.introduction:
A name that means "love" or "beloved" says something simple and true about how a child is welcomed. Some of the world's most enduring names carry that meaning — David, the beloved king; Amy, from the French aimée — alongside lesser-known gems such as Jedidiah, "beloved of Yahweh", the name God gave Solomon.

This guide brings together names meaning love, beloved, dear and affection from Hebrew, Arabic, Sanskrit, Latin, French, Welsh and other languages, for boys and girls, with the meaning and origin of each.
keyTakeaways: David means "beloved" — Jedidiah ("beloved of Yahweh") was Solomon's God-given name (2 Samuel 12:25).
Amy, Mabel and Amanda come from Latin and French words for love and lovable.
Arabic Habib, Habiba and Mahbub mean beloved; Mawadda is the Quran's word for love between spouses (30:21).
Sanskrit Priya means beloved and Prem means love; Welsh Carys means love.

sections.title: Hebrew and biblical names
sections.content: The Hebrew root dwd (beloved) gives David, one of the most popular names in history. Jedidiah, "beloved of Yahweh", is the name the prophet Nathan gave the infant Solomon, and Yedida is its feminine. Ahava is the modern Hebrew word for love.

sections.title: Latin, French and English names
sections.content: Latin amare (to love) and amabilis (lovable) gave rise to several classic names, many of which came to English through Old French. Mabel, a medieval shortening of Amabel, has been revived in recent years.

names.name: Amadeus
names.meaning: Love of God, or loved by God

sections.title: Arabic and Islamic names
sections.content: Arabic has a rich vocabulary of love. Habib (beloved) and its feminine Habiba are classic names; Mahbub and Mahbooba mean "loved". Mawadda, the affection God places between spouses in Quran 30:21 ("He placed between you affection and mercy"), is a lovely, uncommon girls' name. Al-Wadud, "the Loving", is one of the 99 Names of God, which is why the name is usually given as Abdul-Wadud.

sections.title: Sanskrit and Hindi names
sections.content: Sanskrit has many words for love and affection, from the devotional (bhakti, prema) to the tender (sneha). Priya and its variants remain among the most popular Indian girls' names.

sections.title: Celtic and other names
sections.content: Welsh, Irish and other languages add a few beautiful love names. Carys is built on the Welsh word for love, câr; Lev is the Hebrew word for heart (and, coincidentally, the Russian for lion).

sections.title: Choosing a love name
sections.content:
Love names range from the instantly recognisable (David, Amy, Priya) to the rare (Jedidiah, Mawadda, Carys). Familiar names are easy to spell and pronounce; rare ones may need explaining, but the explanation is a pleasant one.

If you are combining traditions, look for pairs that share the meaning: Habiba and Davina, or Priya with an English middle name such as Amy. And as always, check a meaning in more than one source — a few names (Amara, for example) are listed as "love" on some sites with little evidence.
bullets: Familiar: David, Amy, Amanda, Priya, Esme, Mabel.
Rare: Jedidiah, Yedida, Mawadda, Widad, Carys, Ahava.
Check any meaning that appears only on name lists.

faqs.q: What girl names mean love?
faqs.a: Girl names meaning love or beloved include Amy, Amanda, Mabel, Esme, Aimee, Davina, Yedida, Ahava, Habiba, Mahbooba, Mawadda, Priya, Preeti, Sneha and Carys.

faqs.q: What boy names mean love?
faqs.a: Boy names meaning love or beloved include David, Jedidiah, Amadeus, Erasmus, Habib, Mahbub, Prem, Anurag and Pranay.

faqs.q: What does David mean?
faqs.a: David comes from the Hebrew for "beloved". It is the name of the shepherd who became king of Israel.

faqs.q: Which Islamic names mean love?
faqs.a: Habib and Habiba (beloved), Mahbub and Mahbooba (loved), Widad (affection) and Mawadda (affection, from Quran 30:21) are Islamic names connected with love.

faqs.q: Does Amara mean love?
faqs.a: Amara is listed with many meanings online, including "love", but its origin and meaning are not well established. If the meaning matters, choose a name such as Amy or Carys whose meaning is secure.

content.introduction:
The night sky has named children for as long as people have looked up. The moon stands for beauty, calm and the turning of time; stars for guidance, hope and constancy — the pole star that never moves, the morning star that announces the day. Almost every language has given parents a moon name or a star name, and several are now among the most popular names in the world.

This guide gathers celestial names by theme — the moon, moonlight, stars and constellations — from Latin, Greek, Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit and other languages, with the meaning of each and a note on names often mistaken for star names.
keyTakeaways: Luna is No. 18 in BabyCenter's in-progress 2026 girls' table; Aurora is No. 15 for US girls born in 2025 (SSA).
Arabic gives Qamar (moon), Badr (full moon), Hilal (crescent), Najm (star) and Tariq (morning star).
Sanskrit gives Chandra, Soma, Indu and Shashi for the moon, and Tara and Dhruv (pole star) for stars.
Astrid does not mean star — it is Old Norse for "divinely beautiful".

sections.title: Names that mean moon
sections.content: Moon names are found in every tradition. In Greek and Roman myth the moon was a goddess — Selene, and Luna — and Artemis and Diana were linked with her. Arabic has separate words for the moon (qamar), the full moon (badr) and the new crescent (hilal), which marks the start of each Islamic month. Sanskrit has dozens of moon words, several of them popular names.

names.name: Diana
names.meaning: Roman goddess of the moon and the hunt

names.name: Phoebe
names.meaning: Bright; an epithet of the moon goddess

names.name: Cynthia
names.meaning: Epithet of Artemis, from Mount Cynthus

sections.title: Names for moonlight and the moon's beauty
sections.content: Persian and Urdu are especially rich in names built on mah (moon): Mahnoor (light of the moon) is one of the most popular girls' names in Pakistan. Turkish contributes Ayla and Aylin, both linked to the halo of light around the moon, and Arabic has Hala, the moon's halo.

names.name: Ayla
names.meaning: Halo of light around the moon

names.name: Rohini
names.meaning: A nakshatra; the moon's favourite consort in myth

sections.title: Names that mean star
sections.content: Star names have strong religious echoes. Surah 53 of the Quran is an-Najm, "The Star", and Surah 86, at-Tariq, describes the night visitor as a piercing star. In Hindu tradition Dhruva, the steadfast child devotee of Vishnu, became the pole star. And Esther, queen of Persia in the Bible, is usually explained as a Persian word for star.

names.name: Tara
names.note: Irish Tara is an unrelated place name

sections.title: Names from stars and constellations
sections.content: Astronomy has given modern parents a set of bold, short names. Many of the brightest stars have Arabic names, preserved from medieval Islamic astronomy — Altair is from al-ta'ir, "the flyer". Nova, Latin for "new", is the astronomers' word for a star that suddenly brightens; it is in BabyCenter's in-progress 2026 girls' top 40.

names.name: Vega
names.meaning: Bright star in Lyra; from Arabic "the swooping eagle"

names.name: Sirius
names.meaning: Scorching; the brightest star in the night sky

names.name: Atlas
names.meaning: The Titan who holds up the sky

sections.title: Names often mistaken for star names
sections.content:
Astrid is the most common mix-up: it comes from Old Norse Ástríðr, "divinely beautiful", and has nothing to do with Greek astron (star). Stellan, a Swedish name, is likewise unrelated to stella — its meaning is uncertain. Celine is sometimes linked to Selene, but it comes from the Latin name Caelina, connected with caelum, heaven.

If the celestial meaning is the reason for your choice, pick a name where it is secure: Luna, Selene, Stella, Tara, Najm, Qamar, Chandra and Sitara all qualify.
bullets: Astrid — "divinely beautiful", not "star".
Stellan — Swedish, meaning uncertain; not from stella.
Celine — from Caelina (heaven), not Selene (moon).
Irish Tara — a place name, unrelated to Sanskrit Tara (star).

faqs.q: What girl names mean moon?
faqs.a: Girl names meaning moon include Luna, Selene, Diana, Cynthia, Qamar, Hilal, Indu, Purnima, Mahnoor (light of the moon), Mahsa (like the moon), Ayla (moon halo) and Chandni (moonlight).

faqs.q: What boy names mean moon?
faqs.a: Boy names meaning moon include Qamar, Badr (full moon), Hilal (crescent), Chandra, Soma, Shashank, Himanshu and Mahtab (moonlight).

faqs.q: What names mean star?
faqs.a: Names meaning star include Stella, Estelle, Esther, Aster, Tara, Najm, Najma, Sitara, Setareh, Akhtar, Seren and Danica (morning star). Dhruv means the pole star.

faqs.q: Does Astrid mean star?
faqs.a: No. Astrid comes from the Old Norse Ástríðr, meaning "divinely beautiful". The resemblance to Greek astron (star) is coincidental.

faqs.q: Is Luna a popular name?
faqs.a: Yes. Luna is No. 18 in BabyCenter's in-progress 2026 table of US girls' names, which is based on names parents register with BabyCenter during the year.

title: Jewish Baby Names Rooted in the Torah: Meanings and Traditions
subtitle: Patriarchs and matriarchs, prophets, modern Israeli favourites and nature names — with the customs that shape Jewish naming.
excerpt: Jewish baby names with meanings: Torah names like Avraham and Rivka, modern Israeli names like Noa and Eitan, Hebrew nature names, and Jewish naming customs.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Jewish baby names draw on more than three thousand years of Hebrew scripture, rabbinic tradition and the living language of modern Israel. Many families choose a name to honour a relative, to connect a child with a figure from the Torah, or simply to give a name with a clear and beautiful Hebrew meaning.

This guide explains the customs that shape Jewish naming, then lists names in four groups — patriarchs and matriarchs, prophets and other biblical figures, modern Israeli favourites, and nature and blessing names — with the meaning of each. You can read the passages behind the biblical names on Sefaria, which offers the Hebrew Bible with translations.
keyTakeaways: Many Ashkenazi families name a baby after a relative who has died; many Sephardi families honour living grandparents.
Boys are traditionally named at the brit milah on the eighth day; girls are often named in synagogue at a Torah reading.
Many children receive a Hebrew name (used in religious life) as well as an everyday name.
Modern Israeli names such as Noa, Eitan, Omer and Shira draw on biblical and nature words.

sections.title: Naming customs
sections.content:
Two customs shape most Jewish naming decisions. Among Ashkenazi Jews (of Central and Eastern European descent), it is customary to name a baby after a relative who has died, as a way of keeping their memory alive; naming after a living relative is traditionally avoided. Among many Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews, children are often named after living grandparents, which is considered an honour. Families frequently keep only the first letter or the meaning of a relative's name, so a grandfather Moshe might be honoured by a grandson named Max.

Timing is also traditional. A boy is usually named at his brit milah (circumcision) on the eighth day of life. A girl is often named in synagogue when her father or parents are called to the Torah, and many families now also hold a celebration such as a simchat bat. In religious settings a person is called by their Hebrew name and the name of their parent — for example, Yaakov ben Avraham or Rivka bat Sarah.

sections.title: Patriarchs, matriarchs and other Torah names
sections.content: The founding figures of Genesis remain foundational choices, often used in their Hebrew forms in religious families and in English forms elsewhere.

names.name: Shmuel
names.meaning: Name of God; God has heard

sections.title: Modern Israeli names
sections.content: Modern Hebrew has produced a wave of names that feel fresh while staying rooted in the language — many are biblical words or minor biblical names given new life. They are common in Israel and among diaspora families who want a modern Hebrew sound.

names.name: Noa
names.note: Not the same name as Noah

sections.title: Nature and blessing names
sections.content: Many Hebrew names describe the land of Israel or express a hope or blessing. Nili is an acronym from 1 Samuel 15:29 — Netzach Yisrael lo yeshaker, "the Eternal One of Israel does not lie".

sections.title: Hebrew name and everyday name
sections.content:
Many Jewish children outside Israel receive two names: a Hebrew name, used when they are called to the Torah, at their wedding and in prayers for their health, and an everyday name used at school and on documents. The two may be the same (Noah, Sarah), linked by meaning or first letter (Max for Moshe), or entirely different. Some families choose the Hebrew name first, to honour a relative, and then find an everyday name that echoes it.

If you are choosing both, check how the Hebrew name is spelled in Hebrew letters as well as in English, and ask your rabbi about any community customs.

faqs.q: Why do Jewish families name babies after relatives?
faqs.a: In Ashkenazi tradition, babies are often named after a relative who has died, to honour their memory; naming after a living relative is traditionally avoided. Many Sephardi families name children after living grandparents, which is considered an honour.

faqs.q: When is a Jewish baby named?
faqs.a: Boys are traditionally named at the brit milah on the eighth day. Girls are often named in synagogue at a Torah reading, and many families also hold a naming celebration such as a simchat bat.

faqs.q: What is a Hebrew name?
faqs.a: A Hebrew name is the name used in Jewish religious life — for example when called to the Torah — usually combined with a parent's name, such as Yaakov ben Avraham. It may differ from the child's everyday name.

faqs.q: What does Noa mean?
faqs.a: Noa is a Hebrew name meaning "movement". In the Bible it is the name of one of the five daughters of Zelophehad (Numbers 27). It is spelled differently from Noah ("rest") in Hebrew.

title: Sikh Baby Names Inspired by Gurbani: Meanings and the Naam Karan
subtitle: How Sikh names are chosen at the Naam Karan, how they are built from meaningful parts, and popular names with their meanings.
excerpt: Sikh baby names with meanings: how names are chosen through the Guru Granth Sahib at the Naam Karan, the parts Sikh names are built from, and Singh and Kaur.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Sikh baby names are traditionally chosen through the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture. At the naming ceremony, the Naam Karan, the scripture is opened at random and the first letter of the hymn read out becomes the first letter of the child's name. Many Sikh first names are used for both boys and girls; the second name Singh or Kaur, given by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699, marks the difference.

This guide explains the Naam Karan, the meaningful parts that most Sikh names are built from, and a selection of popular names with their meanings. You can read Gurbani with transliteration and translation on SearchGurbani.
keyTakeaways: At the Naam Karan, the name's first letter comes from the hymn read when the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random.
Most Sikh names combine meaningful parts: Gur (Guru), Har (God), Jas (praise), Man (mind) with -preet (love), -jot (light), -deep (lamp), -leen (absorbed).
Many first names are unisex; Singh (lion) and Kaur (princess) indicate male and female.
Guru Gobind Singh gave Singh and Kaur at the founding of the Khalsa in 1699, in part to reject caste surnames.

sections.title: The Naam Karan ceremony
sections.content:
After a baby is born, the family visits the gurdwara for the Naam Karan. Prayers are said, and the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random to read a hukamnama — the Guru's command for the day. The first letter of the first word of that hymn is announced, and the family chooses a name beginning with that letter, which is then shared with the congregation. Karah prashad, the sweet offering, is distributed.

Because the letter comes from the scripture rather than from a list, parents often arrive with a few names in mind for different letters. Practices differ slightly between families and gurdwaras, so ask your local granthi how the ceremony is held.

sections.title: How Sikh names are built
sections.content: Most Sikh names join two meaningful parts, which is why so many share beginnings and endings. Once you know the parts, you can read the meaning of almost any Sikh name.
bullets: Gur- — the Guru: Gurpreet, Gurleen, Gurjot, Gurdeep.
Har- — God: Harjot, Harleen, Harpreet, Harman.
Jas- — praise, glory: Jaspreet, Jasleen, Jasjit.
Man- — mind, heart: Manpreet, Mandeep, Manjot.
Nav- — new: Navjot, Navdeep, Navneet.
-preet — love; -jot — light; -deep — lamp; -leen — absorbed in; -jit/-jeet — victory; -inder — lord.

sections.title: Popular Sikh names and their meanings
sections.content: These names are rooted in the vocabulary of Gurbani. Most can be given to a boy or a girl, with Singh or Kaur completing the name.

sections.title: Singh and Kaur
sections.content:
At Vaisakhi in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa and gave initiated Sikh men the name Singh (lion) and women the name Kaur (usually translated "princess"). The names expressed courage and dignity, and replaced caste-identifying surnames with a shared identity, reflecting the Sikh teaching of equality.

Today many Sikhs use Singh or Kaur as a middle or last name, sometimes alongside a family surname. Because so many first names are unisex, Singh and Kaur also show whether a person is male or female.

faqs.q: How are Sikh babies named?
faqs.a: At the Naam Karan, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random, and the first letter of the hymn read out becomes the first letter of the baby's name. The family then chooses a name beginning with that letter.

faqs.q: What do Singh and Kaur mean?
faqs.a: Singh means "lion" and Kaur is usually translated as "princess". Guru Gobind Singh gave these names in 1699, partly to replace caste surnames with a shared identity.

faqs.q: Are most Sikh names unisex?
faqs.a: Many Sikh first names, such as Gurpreet, Harjot and Simran, are used for both boys and girls. Singh or Kaur usually indicates whether the person is male or female.

faqs.q: What does -preet mean in Sikh names?
faqs.a: Preet means love. Gurpreet means love of the Guru, Manpreet love from the heart, and Jaspreet love of praise.

title: Buddhist Baby Names Reflecting Peace and Wisdom

author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction:
Buddhist baby names often come from Pali and Sanskrit, the classical languages of Buddhist scripture, and from the languages of Buddhist cultures — Tibetan, Thai, Burmese, Sinhala and others. Parents frequently choose names that express the qualities Buddhism values most: loving-kindness, compassion, wisdom and peace.

This guide groups Buddhist names into virtue names, names from the life of the Buddha, and Tibetan and Himalayan names, with the meaning of each. It also explains the difference between a given name and a dharma name, the name a person may receive at a refuge or ordination ceremony. You can read the early texts these names come from on SuttaCentral.
keyTakeaways: Pali and Sanskrit forms differ: Metta/Maitri (loving-kindness), Panna/Prajna (wisdom), Nibbana/Nirvana.
The four "divine abidings" give names: Metta, Karuna (compassion), Mudita (joy) and Upekkha (equanimity).
Tibetan names are often given by a lama; Sherpa families may name children after the day of the week.
A dharma name is received at a refuge or ordination ceremony and is separate from a birth name.

sections.title: Virtue names from Pali and Sanskrit
sections.content: Many Buddhist names are words for qualities cultivated in practice. The four brahmaviharas or "divine abidings" — loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity — are especially loved. Names often exist in a Pali form (used in Theravada countries such as Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar) and a Sanskrit form (used more widely in Mahayana traditions).

sections.title: Names from the life of the Buddha
sections.content: The people around the historical Buddha give a set of meaningful names. Ananda, his cousin and attendant, is remembered for hearing and memorising the teachings; Sujata offered him a bowl of milk-rice before his enlightenment; Khema became one of the foremost nuns.

names.name: Siddhartha
names.meaning: One who has achieved his goal — the Buddha's birth name

names.name: Sujata
names.meaning: Well-born; she offered the Buddha milk-rice

names.name: Yasodhara
names.meaning: Bearer of glory; the Buddha's wife

sections.title: Tibetan and Himalayan names
sections.content: In Tibetan Buddhist communities, a child's name is often given by a lama, and the same names recur widely: Tenzin, "holder of the teachings", is the name of the 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso. Many Tibetan names are unisex. Among Sherpa families, children are often named after the day of the week they were born: Nima (Sunday), Dawa (Monday), Mingma (Tuesday), Lhakpa (Wednesday), Phurba (Thursday), Pasang (Friday) and Pemba (Saturday).

names.name: Dolma
names.meaning: Tara, the female Buddha of compassion

sections.title: Birth names and dharma names
sections.content:
A dharma name is different from a birth name. It is given by a teacher when someone formally takes refuge in the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha, or at ordination as a monk or nun, and it expresses a quality the teacher hopes the student will develop. Lay practitioners may use their dharma name only in a religious setting; monastics usually adopt it fully.

For a baby, families in Buddhist cultures often ask a monk or lama to suggest an auspicious name, and in Thailand many given names are built from Pali and Sanskrit roots. Families outside those cultures should be aware that some words — Bodhi, Nirvana, Karma — carry specific spiritual meanings, and choose them with that in mind.

faqs.q: What are common Buddhist baby names?
faqs.a: Common Buddhist names include Ananda, Bodhi, Metta, Karuna, Shanti and Siddhartha, and Tibetan names such as Tenzin, Pema, Tashi and Dawa.

faqs.q: What is a dharma name?
faqs.a: A dharma name is given by a teacher when someone takes refuge or is ordained. It is separate from the birth name and usually expresses a quality the person aspires to.

faqs.q: Why are many Sherpa children named after days of the week?
faqs.a: In Sherpa tradition, children are often named for the day they were born — Nima for Sunday, Dawa for Monday, Pasang for Friday and so on.

faqs.q: Is Bodhi a good name for a non-Buddhist family?
faqs.a: Bodhi is used internationally as a short, meaningful name. It means "awakening" and has a specific spiritual significance in Buddhism, so families should choose it with that meaning in mind.

title: Choosing an Islamic Baby Name: A Meaning-First Guide
subtitle: How to compare Quranic, Arabic and Muslim names — meaning, origin, transliteration and the limits of popularity lists
excerpt: A meaning-first guide to choosing an Islamic baby name: Quranic versus Arabic names, spelling and pronunciation, and why popularity is no religious verdict.
author: NameVerse Editorial Team
authorCredentials: Compiled from the NameVerse name database and the references cited at the end of this guide

content.introduction: The best Islamic baby name is not necessarily the newest or most popular one. Families may be looking for a Quranic name, a name associated with a prophet or an admired figure, an Arabic word with a good meaning, or a name that travels comfortably across Urdu, Persian, Turkish and English-speaking communities. This guide explains how to compare those choices without treating every Muslim name as if it came from one language or one naming rule.

sections.title: Begin with a good meaning and a clear origin
sections.content: Islamic naming conversations often begin with meaning. A name can be Arabic in origin without being Quranic, and a Muslim family can reasonably choose a Persian, Turkish, Urdu or regional name with a positive meaning. Separate those questions before making a shortlist: What does the name mean in its source language? Is the claimed origin documented? Is the name used in your family or community? NameVerse keeps meaning, origin and religious usage as separate fields because they are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Three useful groups for an Islamic shortlist
sections.content: A shortlist is easier to discuss when it has a shape. Scriptural and prophetic names offer a direct connection to Islamic history. Virtue names express qualities such as patience, generosity, gratitude or courage. Everyday Arabic names may be widely used without appearing in scripture, and that does not make them less meaningful. Compare names within the group that matters to your family instead of assuming that a popularity list can answer a religious question.

sections.title: Check transliteration, script and pronunciation together
sections.content: Arabic script and the Latin alphabet do not map one-to-one. Muhammad, Mohammad, Mohamed and Muhammed are familiar examples of spelling variation; the same issue appears across many names. Before settling on a spelling, ask a fluent speaker how the written form is read, check whether the pronunciation changes in your family language, and decide whether a simplified spelling still represents the form you intend. A profile that shows only one English spelling can give a false impression of certainty.

sections.title: Use popularity as context, not as a religious verdict
sections.content: A name can be popular because it is easy to spell, prominent in a national ranking or newly visible in a media trend. None of those facts establishes whether the name is Quranic, Arabic or appropriate for a particular family. National statistics also do not record religion, so no ranking can tell you which names Muslim families choose. Open the individual profile to inspect the recorded meaning, origin and script before treating a list position as evidence.

faqs.q: Does an Islamic baby name have to appear in the Quran?
faqs.a: No. Muslim families use Quranic names, names of prophets and companions, Arabic names with good meanings, and names from Persian, Turkish, Urdu and other cultures. Quranic appearance is one possible preference, not the definition of every Islamic name.

faqs.q: Are Arabic and Muslim names the same thing?
faqs.a: No. Arabic describes a language and cultural tradition; Muslim describes religious usage. Many Muslim names are Arabic, but Muslim families also use names from other languages, and many Arabic names are not specifically religious.

faqs.q: Why are there several spellings of the same Muslim name?
faqs.a: Arabic script represents sounds differently from the Latin alphabet, and transliteration systems vary. Regional pronunciation and inherited family spelling also matter, so several English spellings can refer to one underlying form.

faqs.q: How should I check a name before choosing it?
faqs.a: Check the source-language meaning and origin, listen to a fluent speaker say it, review the script and spelling variants, and ask trusted family or community members about local associations. Treat numerology and lucky-number claims as traditional beliefs rather than evidence about the name.

content.introduction: Hindu naming traditions are diverse rather than uniform. A family may choose a Sanskrit word, a name of a deity or epic figure, a regional form, a family name, or a name selected in relation to a birth-star or other customary practice. The meaning matters, but so do pronunciation, local usage and the context a name carries for the people who will say it every day.

sections.title: Sanskrit is a source language, not a complete category
sections.content: Many Hindu names have Sanskrit roots, but a Sanskrit origin alone does not tell you how a name is used today. Regional languages reshape pronunciation and spelling, and the same word may carry different associations in different communities. When comparing a name, record its source language separately from its religious or cultural use. That distinction makes a profile more useful than a simple label such as “Indian name.”

sections.title: Devotional names and the story behind them
sections.content: Names connected with deities, epics and devotional poetry often carry a story as well as a dictionary meaning. Parents may choose an epithet because of a quality it represents, a family tradition or a festival association. Read the full form and its context before shortening it: a nickname may be convenient, but it can hide the historical or theological connection that attracted the family in the first place.

sections.title: Birth traditions are personal and regional
sections.content: Some families consult a priest, astrologer or elders about a starting sound, rashi or nakshatra; others choose a name independently or combine a traditional name with a modern nickname. There is no single practice that represents every Hindu family. If a starting syllable matters to you, confirm the convention with the person or community guiding your ceremony instead of relying on a generic internet table.

sections.title: Test the name in the languages your child will hear
sections.content: A name that looks simple in English may have a different stress pattern in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, Telugu or another family language. Say it aloud with the surname, write the intended script if one is important, and ask relatives to pronounce the spelling without coaching. Popularity can show what is visible in a national dataset, but it cannot tell you whether a particular regional pronunciation feels natural.

faqs.q: What makes a name Hindu?
faqs.a: Families may describe a name as Hindu because it is connected with Sanskrit, a deity, an epic, a virtue, a devotional tradition or a community naming practice. The label is contextual; a Sanskrit origin by itself does not describe every way a name is used.

faqs.q: Do Hindu baby names need to be Sanskrit?
faqs.a: No. Sanskrit names are common, but families also choose names from regional languages, family traditions and contemporary usage. The right choice depends on the meaning and cultural connection that matter to your family.

faqs.q: What are rashi and nakshatra naming rules?
faqs.a: They are customary systems that associate a child’s birth details with sounds or syllables considered suitable for a name. Practices vary by family and region, so use a trusted practitioner or elder if you want to follow one rather than treating a generic list as authoritative.

faqs.q: How can I check the meaning of a Sanskrit name?
faqs.a: Check the word in a reliable language or naming reference, compare the transliteration and pronunciation, and ask a fluent speaker how the word is understood today. A profile should distinguish a literal translation from a devotional or modern association.

title: Christian Baby Names from the Bible

seoKeywords: Christian baby names from the Bible

content.introduction: Christian naming draws from more than one layer of history. Some families choose a name that appears in the Bible; others prefer a saint, a virtue, a church calendar connection or a name inherited from a grandparent. Biblical names themselves often arrive through Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek and Latin forms, so a familiar English spelling may be one step in a longer transmission history.

sections.title: Biblical does not mean one language or one style
sections.content: The Bible contains names preserved in different languages and manuscript traditions. English forms such as John, Mary, Peter and James sit alongside Hebrew forms, Greek forms and later Latin spellings. When a profile says that a name is biblical, check whether it refers to a person in scripture, a translated form, or a later Christian tradition built around that person. That detail explains why several apparently different names can share a historical root.

sections.title: Meaning, namesake and tradition are separate questions
sections.content: A biblical name can appeal because of its literal meaning, the story of its namesake or the virtues a church community associates with it. Those are related but not identical reasons. For example, a family may choose a name to honour a biblical figure even when the everyday English meaning is not the main attraction. A careful shortlist records the linguistic meaning and the religious context side by side.

sections.title: Consider saints, virtues and family history too
sections.content: Christian naming is not limited to a biblical index. Saint names, virtue names and names passed through a congregation or family can be just as important. If a baptismal or confirmation name is part of your tradition, ask the relevant church about its local practice. A name can have a biblical root and a distinctly regional pronunciation, so community usage is worth recording rather than flattening into a single “correct” form.

sections.title: Choose a spelling that your family can carry
sections.content: Classic names still develop spelling and pronunciation differences across languages. Say the name with the surname, check the form used in your church or family, and decide whether a traditional spelling or a modern variant feels more honest to your history. National popularity rankings can help you understand how familiar a form is in the United States, but they do not measure spiritual significance or tell you which tradition your family should follow.

faqs.q: Does a Christian baby name have to be in the Bible?
faqs.a: No. Some Christian families prefer biblical names, while others choose saints’ names, virtue names, family names or names that simply carry a positive meaning. Church and family traditions differ.

faqs.q: Why do biblical names have different spellings?
faqs.a: Names moved between Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, Latin and later European languages. Translation choices and local pronunciation produced familiar variants such as John and Juan or Mary and Maria.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a biblical name and a saint name?
faqs.a: A biblical name refers to a person or word in the Bible. A saint name may honour a later Christian figure; some saint names are also biblical, but the two categories are not identical.

faqs.q: How should I evaluate a claimed biblical meaning?
faqs.a: Look for the source language and the historical person or word behind the claim. Popular name lists sometimes compress a complex etymology into one slogan, so compare a documented meaning with the story or tradition that makes the name meaningful to your family.
